speakeroldname: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: SHIPPING OF CANADIAN CREWS ON FOREIGN VESSELS
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for
Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) asked me a certain question relating to the possibility of shipping Canadian crews on United States fishing vessels on the Atlantic coast and I promised I would give a statement today.
The shipping of Canadian crews to American fishing vessels on the Atlantic coast is governed by an act of parliament, the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act. Section 10 of that act provides for the forfeiture of every foreign fishing vessel which has entered Canadian territorial waters for any purpose not permitted by treaty or by any law of Great Britain or of Canada. So far as United States fishing vessels are concerned there is a law of Canada, namely, an order in council under the authority of section 3 of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, chapter 43, R.S.C., under which a licence may be issued to a United States fishing vessel enabling it to

Canadair Limited
enter any port on the Atlantic coast of Canada for the purpose of purchasing bait, ice, seines, lines and all other supplies and outfits. The present order in council, P.C. 3955, September 24, 1946, does not permit the shipping of crews on foreign vessels.
Since the United States vessel in question the Gertrude de Costa is now in the port of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, with bait and ice on board, the governor in council, under section 3 of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, is issuing a licence to this vessel to permit it to ship necessary complement of crew at the port of Lunenburg. While granting a licence in this special case it should be understood that this concession is in no way to be considered as a precedent.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It would be impossible for me to answer the hon. gentleman's question without knowing the contents of the parcel. I might say that on a twenty pound gift parcel, which is the maximum allowed for such a parcel, the rate to England is $2.50, made up as follows: England gets a credit of 51 cents on each of these parcels which the British postal authorities deliver anywhere in England. We have to pay them that 51 cents. The shipping companies charge us $1.50 per two cubic feet, which is about the space of a gift parcel of 20 pounds, takes up. Mr. Chairman, just a sentence or two to add to what I was saying yesterday on clause 1, which reads:
This act may be cited as the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947.
The inference from the title is that the measure before us is one to enable a continuation of certain policies that have been in effect. Our whole quarrel with the government, which we have been trying to state on behalf of the Canadian people, is that they are not continuing for a sufficiently long enough period the policies in relation to the cost of living which the Canadian people want continued.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that this clause is to stand?

In asking that this clause stand, the minister said there might be some amendments after the schedule had been adopted. But on the actual clause itself, aside from any amendments to the schedule, I should like to make a few comments and also to move an amendment in regard to ministerial control over these control powers. I have not wasted any of the time of the house in speaking on controls because the people I represent are completely in favour of the present policy. I have received a large number of communications from both the working people and white collar people that I represent, and without exception they have advocated the continuation of these controls over the essentials of life, therefore I say I am for these controls, but for controls in which there is the essence of parliamentary control.
The member for Kootenay West last week spoke very well in answer to some of the arguments that had been put up by the Progressive Conservative party who had called these controls tyranny and despotism. He said that they could not be considered tyranny or despotism so long as in the end the government had to return to parliament, as the government is doing now, for power to continue the controls. Charges of bureaucracy have been made by the opposition, and civil servants who
have done a difficult job exceedingly well have been loosely slandered by such charges. Some of these men in public office may have got swelled heads and found a little authority too much for them to handle. But in the life of this great dominion do we not find similar characters in every field? You find them here in the House of Commons. For example, we have all seen men who because they happen to be sitting on the front benches opposite think they have the privileges and prerogatives of ministers of the crown. Therefore I see no reason why this whole programme should be scathingly denounced as bureaucracy because of a few failings of officials administering them.
There is, however, I think a great difference between the attitude of the Liberal party to these controls and the attitude of our friends of the C.C.F. party. The charge is made that we are one on this. I think that charge is wrong, because the very essential of controls by this government, as pointed out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his apt quotation of Professor Lower, is that there should be in the end parliamentary control and responsibility by the ministers to the people who are sent here to represent them.
I may be wrong in this, and if I am wrong I shall accept immediate correction by the C.C.F. My feeling is that if they were in power they would be quite content to set up these super planning boards and experts of the type of Professor Laski and leave them to do the job remote from any parliamentary control.
No.

I am going to accept that correction and I am also going to explain why I made this apparent error. As hon. members know, at times I am labelled as being almost too close to the C.C.F. party. Whenever a member of that party speaks I move down near them so that I can catch every word in order to understand what he is driving at. As British Columbia members know, I am in considerable sympathy with many of their objectives. I do the same thing when any member of the Social Credit party is speaking. Being a keen student I have, however, been bewildered at times by some of the things said by apparently responsible people of the C.C.F. party.
Last week the members of the C.C.F. party in British Columbia held a convention in Vancouver. I read in the Vancouver Sun a
Emergency Powers

report of that convention, and I found the following on the front page of the issue of Friday, April 11:
First task of a C.C.F. administration would be the swift removal of the major sources of wealth production from private hands. This was the declaration today of Colin Cameron, provincial president of the C.C.F. in his report prepared for delivery to the party's annual convention in Hotel Vancouver.
"It must be made clear," Mr. Cameron continued, "that our whole programme of social services and economic extension rests on that first bold revolutionary bid."
This is not a misquotation, because it is taken from a prepared report which he turned over to the press beforehand. I understand that.
Head it all.

We have heard so much of that in British Columbia; I have heard so much of it that I understand it. Then we heard the excellent speech made in the house yesterday afternoon by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I heard the excellent speech made here by the hon. member for Swift Current, and how far apart they are from the speech of Mr. Cameron! Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Swift Current said, as reported at page 2109 of Hansard.
We do believe in private enterprise, and we do not believe in the little private enterpriser being controlled by the freebooting monopoly enterprisers who control and own so much in this country.
The hon. member said: "We do believe in private enterprise", as did the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I also listened to the hon. member for Halifax, and these two speeches by the members for Halifax and Moose Jaw could have been made by the same man. The hon, member for Yorkton charged that all business men were Jesse Jameses, a lovely phrase which he cribbed from the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I could not tell the difference between the speech of the hon. member for Halifax and the hon. member for Moose Jaw, both good business men; for when the member for Moose Jaw spoke to the people of Saskatchewan, according to the Regina Leader-Post, he was for private enterprise. His speech was carried last Friday in the Regina Leader-Post in one column, and slam-bang against it was an account of Colin Cameron's revolutionary speech at Vancouver. If I made a little mistake in listening to everything that hon. members of the C.C.F. party-said about planners they must forgive me for this confusion. Colin Cameron is the provincial president of the C.C.F. party in British

Columbia, and was formerly a member of the legislature. In a kindly way I am going to make a suggestion, because as I listened to the Social Credit party's most excellent suggestion the other night-I sat close to them and I think the members of the Social Credit party will do me the justice of saying that I listened to them-

Thank you very much. This is my first speech on controls. Second, the C.C.F. quickly rose to my bait by saying that I was wrong. I was explaining why I was wrong. I was wrong because I was misinformed by their several attitudes. I wish to say that I hope the attitude they may take in the future will not mislead us who are seekers after truth and who are confused when one responsible man of the C.C.F. party says one thing and another says another thing about the same thing.
A few nights ago the hon. member for Lethbridge was speaking. I was down in that corner trying to find out all I could about the Social Credit philosophy, and at times I find it diificult, although he is a lucid and clear speaker. He was challenged by the hon, member for Cape Breton South; and in return he said: "I challenge any member of the C.CJ'. party or any other party to say whether any responsible members of this group", speaking of his own group, had advocated such and such a course. The hon. member for Cape Breton South wanted to know who were the responsible and who were the irresponsible members of that group so that we would know who are the prophets and teachers of the true

Emergency Powers
gospel, and who were the prophets teaching heresy. I would suggest to the C.C.F. and the Social Credit parties that henceforth in the Parliamentary Guide they put a little asterisk before the names of those who are responsible and who speak with responsibility, and leave the asterisk off those who are irresponsible-

May I ask the hon. member
a question?
Yes.
Would it not take a fairsized revolution to give us free private enterprise in this country?
The hon. member had best direct his question to the hon. member for Swift Current who is sitting behind him, because he said he believes in it. Let him read it again.
He knows it is not here.
He says he believes in it. Ask him for a full explanation of it, since he has such a deep and implicit belief in it.
I shall be glad to give it some time.

However, I turn to the C.C.F. bible, to know whether to believe Colin Cameron, the president of the C.C.F. in British Columbia, or those C.C.F. gentlemen who speak as I do in the house, the hon. member for Swift Current and the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I turn to "Make This Your Canada". There are no asterisks in it; therefore I take it it is responsible so far as the C.C.F. party is concerned. At the end of the Regina manifesto we find the following:
_ No C.C.F. government will rest content until it has eradicated capitalism.
Tie that in with private enterprise and with the speeches made in the House of Commons by the two members to whom I have referred. In the House of Commons, members of the C.C.F. party say they believe in private enterprise. They are in the same class as the hon. member for Stanstead who can vote both ways.
I apologize for being so wrong in misunderstanding the C.C.F. position, but let me get back to section 2 of the bill. I believe positively in parliamentary control, in responsibility of the ministers not only for acts committed in their department but for acts committed by any agency of the crown under them. In the consolidation of the orders in council there are some orders in council which have explicit definitions of the powers and 83166-136
responsibilities of the ministers, those of the Minister of Finance and those of the Minister of Fisheries for example. In other orders in council the powers of the ministers-I put it kindly-are but implicit; and there is no mention at all of the powers of the minister in a few of the orders. I say that somewhere we as a parliament, the court of last resort in this country, must have a man who is responsible for acts by these various boards and bureaux. The fact that it appears in some of the orders in council in the schedule is not sufficient; it should appear right in the bill itself.
Which bill?

Bill 104. I have known the hon. member for Lake Centre for a long time. I admire and respect him greatly. He made an impassioned speech yesterday and mentioned the denial of the right of individuals to appeal to the courts of the land against rulings of the various boards. I was swayed by that. I listened to him attentively and I can see why he has made such great success at the bar, because if you put twelve Saskatchewan farmers in the box and let the hon. member for Lake Centre at them he will win his case. The difference between parliament and a jury box is that the next morning we can read Hansard. I read Hansard, and when I read his remarks to the effect that we are tyrants who have removed that last liberty, the right of appeal to the highest court of the land, I thought of some reading that I did last winter with regard to the early days of workmen's compensation in my province. That legislation was introduced by a Liberal government and bitterly opposed by the Tories, especially by lawyers and insurance companies. Oh, the lawyers waxed indignant about that removal from the poor, humble injured working man of the precious right to appeal from a dictatorial workmen's compensation board in respect of unjust awards. How they bled for the workingman 1 Well, workmen's compensation has rolled on all these years, and the workmen of British Columbia have been well protected and have saved many needless legal fees. There is ministerial responsibility to the act because the minister of labour in the provincial legislature is held responsible for any injustice which may have been done by the workmen's compensation board.
The same can be said of the Canadian pension board, again described as a body from which there is no appeal to the courts of the land. But who is the man that must carry the responsibility in this House of Commons, the greatest and highest court of appeal, for seeing that justice is done in all the rulings of

Emergency Powers

the board? Who is that man but the Minister of Veterans Affairs? For that reason I say that we are not denying to those who may feel that they are unfairly dealt with by the boards the right to appeal to the highest court in the land, just so long as it is clearly understood by the people that here in parliament there is one man responsible for each of these boards, one man who must justify before a gathering of his peers the actions of the board.
The second reason concerns the public outlook. There is an old saying-I need hardly repeat it, though it is important-that not only must justice be done but it must be known that justice is done; and certainly if it is known by an amendment written into the bill, known to the people of Canada, that these are not bureaucrats surrounded with absolute power but still servants of the people, that there is still one man, in this house, of the servants of the people, who must answer for the actions of the board, then the people can be assured that justice will be done.
The third reason comes closer perhaps to members of parliament. There is, I will not say a tendency but at least a temptation, for some ministers, when you go to them-not in the House of Commons but in their offices- and protest against actions of boards, to say, "Oh, well, the boards have been set up to run their own affairs, and we cannot do anything". To remove that temptation from ministers I would like to see clearly in the bill an amendment stating that the minister shall not only have control but shall be responsible. With that in mind I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), the following amendment to section 2, a new subsection 2(1):
Wherever the word minister is used in the schedule to this act, the rights, powers, duties, liabilities and functions of that minister shall extend and apply to such boards, and other public bodies, officers, subjects, services and properties of the crown as may be designated or assigned to the minister by the governor in council over which the minister shall have the control, regulation, management and supervision.
The wording of that, as you will realize, is not my own. It is taken directly from the powers of the minister in the most recent departmental act, that of reconstruction and supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to compliment the hon. member on his contribution to the debate and would ask that his suggestion stand for consideration by the officers of my department and by the government. I would

point out that in one of the orders in the schedule at page 23, is found a clause which reads:
In the exercise of its powers conferred by these regulations or otherwise, the board shall be responsible to the minister and, whenever any directions are given by the minister, all action taken by the board shall be in accordance with such directions.
Generally speaking when I was Minister of Finance I tried to see that clauses of that kind were inserted in the orders which set up the boards that operated under my jurisdiction, and I am in accord with the general principle of my hon. friend's observations. I should point out, however, that the language of his amendment may be too sweeping, and it is for that reason that I should like to have the proposal stand. There is a class of organization which should not, I submit, be subject to the direction of the minister and that is any organization which is in the nature of a court. For instance, in some bf these orders courts of rental appeal and the like are set up. These probably should not be subject to the direction of the minister; they should have independent jurisdiction. The same may be true of certain organizations connected with labour relations It may be they should not be subject to interference by the minister. But with regard to organizations of the type of the wartime prices and trade board, it is perfectly proper that they should be subject to direction from the minister, and that probably is recognized by the clause which I have read, which appears in the wartime prices regulations.
With regard to this section, I suggest that at some stage it should be allowed to stand. I do not think the section can be passed, either with or without this amendment, at the present time, but should stand until we get through the schedule, as I explained yesterday. If however hon. members have any suggestions to make as to the proposal itself, this may be as good a time as any to make them. If they are made now it will give the government an opportunity to consider them before we return to the section.

I have no suggestions at the moment with regard to the section, but I do wish to reply to some of the remarks made by the member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). First may I say that I have admired the independent stand that he has taken in this house on numerous occasions, although perhaps there is a reason for that show of independence. He did not, however, deal fairly in this case with the quotation he gave from the Canadian Press report of Mr. Cameron's speech. He read a sentence and

Emergency Powers
stopped there, whereas the sentence he read was only a part, really only half of what Mr. Cameron said.
It was the end of a paragraph.
It was not the end of a paragraph either.
In the Vancouver Sun it was the end of the paragraph.
I have it, and it is the same Canadian Press article.

Mine was in the Vancouver Sun, Friday, April 11, front page, not by the Canadian Press but by the Vancouver Sun, and the remarks ended at the end of the paragraph. I am not here to read the entire speech. A paragraph is one coherent thought.
Whose paragraph?
The paragraph in the press release that was given by Mr. Cameron.
The Vancouver Sun is not above distorting news any more than any other capitalist paper in Canada.
The old cry of the C.C.F., "We were misquoted".
It is not a misquotation, but the hon. gentlemen did not finish the quotation. Let me read it.
Give us the whole speech.
Yes. I will give you what is in the press, and I will not stop just where you stopped for your own convenience to make your own case.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: What paper is it?
The Leader-Post, Regina, Saskatchewan, April 12, 1947-a good Liberal paper.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is a good paper.
It is a good paper of the kind.
Who said so?

Let me quote it.
"Our whole programme of social services and economic extension rests on that first bold revolutionary bid," he said. "If we present effectively the case for sane and intelligent revolutionary progress through use of democratic procedure and institutions, we can hope in Can-83166- 136i
ada to lay foundations of that free classless society which is the goal of all socialist aspirations.
Through our democratic institutions. The C.C.F. has never at any time gone beyond the use of democratic institutions, or as is the phrase they use in Great Britain, revolution by consent. If there is confusion in C.C.F. speeches, the same confusion results from listening to speeches from the other side of the house. For instance, the Minister of Justice in presenting this bill made the statement that the policy of the government was to get back as quickly as possible to a free economy. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said that the policy of -the government was to get back as quickly as possible to a free economy. But let us get the opinion of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) on a free economy. He does not think a great deal of a free economy; indeed he does not think it is anything worth while getting back to.
He is not a minister.

Perhaps the reason he is not a minister is that he holds these ideas. The reason that the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) is not closer to the ministerial seats is because he holds similar ideas. The front benches are not very keen on ideas.
On page 2056 of Hansard we find the hon.
member for Spadina saying:
During the war the government used successfully the device of controls to divert the tremendous output of industry to the interests of the state-which at that time was the fullest prosecution of the war. Now in these critical and emergent years of peace we must take the same forces and use them, but not, as some political thinkers would suggest, to bring industry back to normal.
The political thinkers he possibly had in mind were the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who wish to get back as quickly as possible to a free economy. The hon. member for Spadina continues:
To my mind that is a label only, and one which hides a _ multitude of iniquities. As we saw in the thirties, in the titanic struggle of economic forces, the small man was crushed.
That is, under a free economy in Canada prior to the war the small man was crushed.
Oh, oh.

All right; I am quoting the hon. member for Spadina.
Emergency Powers
We do not know whether they are your words or his.
The lawyers would starve to death.

No lawyer will ever starve to death under capitalism. There are too many crooks to defend. The hon. member for Spadina said further:
After all, it is not the function of either the landlord or the millowner to run his business for the benefit of the public. The true function, as they see it, is to produce profits; and it would be naive for us to assume otherwise, or to ask them to run their business in an altruistic manner. The good business man is not operating for the sake of charity; and if scarcity presents him with an opportunity, he takes advantage of it.
That is the system under which we are living, where the need of one individual is used to the advantage of another. That is what the C.C.F. wants to get away from.
Then on page 2057 the hon. member for Spadina has this to say-and I should like to know how many on that side of the house agree with him. I should like to see the hon. member for Vancouver North get up and take issue with him in this matter. I quote:
Many of these people reason that Hitler and Mussolini imposed a controlled economy on their countries and that all kinds of evils followed as a natural result-loss of liberty, persecution, regimentation, mass murder and war. They are convinced that if we hold on to the few controls that remain we shall be selling the freedom of this country down the river-quite overlooking the fact that Britain, probably the most largely controlled English speaking country in the world today, is also the one in which the flame of freedom burns the brightest. Only persons who have little faith in democracy should live in fear of democratic controls. People have come to take for granted the exercise of economic controls which prior to the war they would have called totalitarian. We must not forget that the little people of this country do not merely accept controls; they actually want them, and they do not want to go back to the days of false booms and real depressions.
I will answer. The hon. member invited my comments.
No, I did not invite them but I have no objection to the hon. member making them at the proper time.
Oh, let us get on with the work.

Let my hon. friends be fair in this matter. Yesterday when the discussion began, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) started a discussion something like this on section 1, but was ruled out of order by the Chairman. I am not now

disagreeing with the Chairman's ruling, but my impression was that if there was any section in the bill on which there could be general discussion, it was on section 1, the title. But this section deals with this specific point, and the hon. member for Vancouver North was allowed to proceed. My hon. friends did not object. They were enjoying it very much.
Because he moved an amendment.
I know the hon. member moved an amendment, but what he said in moving the amendment was not related to what he said in the first part of his speech.
The hon. member's party were very kind to me. They said "explain", and I explained.

No, the party did not say anything of the kind. The purpose was to create a false impression of what was said by a member of the C.C.F., and we are not going to allow the hon. member to get away with that sort of thing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I might say to the hon. member for Vancouver East that I was asked for a ruling with regard to section 2. I made a ruling that in my opinion it allowed very wide latitude-it deals with all the orders in council-and I did not see how I could rule the hon. member out of order. I thought I was right and still think I was right.

I rise to speak on section 2. I have not taken up much time in connection with this bill, and I speak now because I must be at a meeting of the committee on railways at four o'clock.
I wish to refer to two or three principles in connection with controls. I wish to speak about three items which, if continued in new form will afford no relief so far as I see. The other day I referred to what has been done in the United States regarding production. That was the key to the solution of control and decontrol in that great country. Sooner or later we in Canada would have to follow suit, in view of the fact that our economy is closely interlocked with that of the United States. In the United States figures show that they are now having their greatest volume of production in all their history of all classes of goods. The result has been that that production has had a great deal to do with maintaining and aiding consumer goods business, and in some instances in lowering prices. This has been the effect, either directly or indirectly, of their decontrol policy.

Emergency Powers
This whole matter gets back very largely to the law of supply and demand, the principle which applied long before the war and which made the United States the great country it is. In some respects let me say that the public holds relief in this respect in its own hands. It need not buy manufactured goods offered in the stores at higher prices if it does not want to. That is shown in the large departmental stores throughout the country today. Clothing for men and women is being offered at fabulous prices-and in this I include men's ties, shirts and all sorts of things. The same applies to women's clothes. Some of these articles will not be bought at higher prices, and in many instances the result has been that the goods have remained on the counters, with few if any people buying them.
The Minister of Finance dealt with two or three controls the other day. I believe some reference was made by him to re-control where necessary. It was pointed out by me that in the coming winter it may be necessary to give some relief in order to make fuel available. This winter we still have snow in April, and when the warmer weather does come we shall have had about nine months of winter weather, when some fuel must be provided. The minister said that they might find it necessary to reestablish, if urgent and necessary, some forms of control.
Then I think something further should be done in connection with milk, because any neglect in this respect might have a severe effect on the health of our younger population. I should hope that next winter the minister might see fit to reestablish some system of a moderate milk subsidy for the winter months at least.
In connection with section 2 of the bill I should like to see some amendment in respect of the orders and regulations affecting houses. The present system of controls has retarded the building of houses, so that no one now wants to invest in real estate. In the city from which I come, sixty-five per cent of the people used to own their own homes. Many have lost them to the mortgagees. Some of the owners have had undesirable tenants under this system of controls, tenants who have misused the properties and left them in such a rack and ruin state that insurance companies would not pay a dollar in the event of fire. I know of one instance where the mortgagee wanted to foreclose. He asked for a further payment of principal because of the way undesirable tenants ruined his investment.
I do not favour a form of control under which an owner cannot get into his own house, even after years of waiting; it is nothing
but state confiscation. Where the tenant had no lease he could be put out. The rental regulations are ridiculous and have worked great hardships on returned soldiers who have not been able to get into their own houses on which they had spent their gratuities and credits.
I suggest that the minister should have some form of federal inspection. I know that in my city the offices are filled with rental administrators. They have had to move to a larger building at 32 Adelaide street. It may be that only five or ten per cent of these undesirable cases would require further investigation by federal authority. Why could not a check be made on undesirable tenants so that the landlord would have a little encouragement and a chance to put them out, and would be prepared to invest more money in real estate?
How can this be administered from Ottawa? I say it should be turned over to the provinces and municipalities for rent control regulation, if necessary. The municipalities regulate the building of houses and have control of fire and building by-laws. Why should the dominion attempt to operate a system like this, away down here in Otta-wa, and discourage the building of houses for all time to come?
I do urge upon the government that some further regulation be applied to housing along the lines I have suggested, and that they be made to apply to those undesirable tenants who came in, destroyed property, ruined it to the point where it has to be rebuilt from the ground up by a landlord who may lose it. Why should this be allowed? It is nothing but confiscation.
As I have said, only five or ten per cent of the tenants could be considered as undesirable. Inspection could be made of them under civic by-law. If the federal power cannot do it, then let the property inspector, the building inspector or the fire chief visit these places and take note of the inflammable material which has been collected.
Why should not the municipal and city police continue this process of housing control, if there is to be any control? It would be far better to put an end to control altogether, and apply the system I have suggested.

I want to be sure I am
in order, and so I refer to the section under discussion; it is section 2, having to do with orders and regulations continued in force.
I rise to make a few brief comments, and to make reference to the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). I know he has been well answered already, but there are one or two further comments
Emergency Powers

in that connection which I feel ought to be made. The hon. member began by referring to the view expressed by some that there was no difference between the C.C.F. and the Liberal party in the matter of controls. But he proceeded to dissociate himself from that idea, and to show that there is a difference. He said his understanding was that the C.C.F. party would deliberately appoint bodies to take charge of public functions, which bodies would have no contact with governmental control through representation in parliament.
Of course the hon. member knew we would deny that immediately. Then he proceeded to quote. In the first place, let me say to him he may find there are many people in the ranks of the C.C.F. who are no more proud of being associated with the Liberal party than he is of being associated with us. I would point out further to him that the quotation he made had nothing whatever to do with the principle of control. Neither of the gentlemen he quoted was making any reference to controls or to the appointment of bodies to carry out certain important functions, or to the mechanism by which democratic control might be mainatined. Neither was discussing that.
I suggest the reason for the first quotation, that from the presidential address of Mr. Cameron in Vancouver, was that Mr. Cameron had used the word "revolution." That is the reason it was used.
I believe that perhaps the best thing any man or woman in the house can contribute to the public life of Canada is a point of view, whether that point of view be individually expressed or be expressed as the view of an organized body. Because I believe that I do not desire to have the views I hold either misrepresented or distorted. I want my views to be considered for what they are and not have somebody's distortion of them.
The word "revolution" is a perfectly good word and I do not propose to give it up just because somebody misinterprets it. If it stands for blood and horror to my hon. friends on the government side of the house or in any part of the house, then they do not understand their English, that is all. If I had the time I could give the committee numerous examples of revolutionaries in art, science, religion and, in fact, in every walk of human life. I could show how Watt himself, the man who discovered the power which originated the industrial revolution, was a revolutionist in industry. There have been revolutionists in music and in art. Jesus Christ was a revolutionist in religion and of course they crucified him. I

have no doubt that the Liberal party would crucify him today if he came back, and maybe a lot on this side would help them.
Revolution means a fundamental change in human 'affairs, and that is all it means. We happen to stand for revolution by the consent of the people through our democratic institutions.
You will never get it.

My hon. friend says we will never get it. He is a real revolutionist of the bloody sort, but I am revolutionist of the democratic kind. If we do not get it in that way, I do not want it and lam not interested in it. I am interested in the revolution that is brought iabout witih the consent of the Canadian people at the ballot box and without any of the misrepresentation that we had this afternoon.
There is no contradiction between the man who believes in free private enterprise and the man who believes in the necessity for a great revolutionary change in this country's way of doing business and in this country's way of life. As I suggested in my question to my hon. friend a moment ago, there could be no greater revolution possible in this country than the one that would leave every individual free to express his own being and his own personality and to do the kind of work he wants to do and to make his contribution to society. That would be revolution. There are few individuals that have any such freedom today.
To believe in that is to have a very idealistic concept indeed. As the hon. member for Swift Current said, an ideal of that sort is pretty much like the ideal of those who hope to get to heaven. It' is an ideal but it is far from being the fact in Canadian life today. So thus goes the argument of my hon. friend. I do not know why he brought' it up. He may have had some idea in his own mind. I do not think he inteded to misrepresent the viewpoint of this group, but I conclude by saying: Let those in this house oppose the C.C.F. all they want to, provided that they oppose us for what we really are, for what we stand for. I resent being opposed because of something in which I never believed or advocated.

speechtext: May I suggest that the section stand and that we go on to another section.
I have something to say.

Louder.

Carried.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Start anywhere.

You are going to get something in a minute that is worth while. This government is not so good that it can laugh a't everything. I think a lot of the fellows over there really do not know where they are going. There are a lot of others on that side, on the back benches, who have more in them than those on the front benches, and there are a lot on this side who have more in them than those who are on the front benches.
I asked for a return last year giving the number of people in the employ of the government of Canada. That is very important, is it not?-the people who are in our employ. I just want to tell those fellows who are sitting on the government benches that there are too many people trying to look after too few in this country right now. You just cannot get away from that. We have to get down to brass tacks; and I am going to give a few figures.
Oh. oh.

You fellows over there can laugh if you want to. A member of the cabinet the other day referred to the amount of income tax he had to pay. Let us get down to something here; let us get busy and get something done. Let us have on the front benches more fellows like that bright young boy in the back seat over there, who is not as incompetent and inept as many of the leading lights on the front benches, who are probably there for political purposes and for nothing else. I have some good friends-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Why?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I ruled that we would allow wide latitude in the discussion of section 2, but it must be discussion with respect
to the bill under consideration and with respect to the orders in council which are set forth in the schedule. I do not think it allows discussion of the income tax or some other legislation.

I bow to your ruling and I will keep as close as I can to the text of my sermon. A lot of people have talked about this bill as being the bill of fifty-seven varieties, copying Heinz. It is not that at all; it is Canada's greatest fruit salad. Without exception, it is the silliest, the most foolish bill that has ever been brought into this House of Commons. If you want me to quote my authority, it is my friend the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). If anybody knows anything about bills, he does.
I have a few figures to put on Hansard, and I think they will surprise hon. members. I wonder if each individual minister would like to know the increased numbers on the payroll of bis department today. I have a return here showing what a great increase there has been in the number of government employees, and while on the subject of returns I put this to the committee:	Can we get a
return that is reliable brought down in this House of Commons? This affects the whole people of Canada and it affects everything that is in this bill. I had a return brought down last year to show the number of people in the employ of Canada and how much we are paying them; and what do you think, Mr. Chairman? - four departments, employing 8,600 people, were left out of that return! On March 31, 1946, we had in round figures 155,000 persons in the employ of the government of Canada. The return was short by about 7,000 employees, but what is 7,000 or 10,000 to an administration so incompetent and inept as I see sitting in front of me at the present time? It makes no difference to them at all. But I am Scotch and a lot of other fellows in this country are Scotch and they like to bite a nickel a couple of times before they spend it.
On March 31, 1946, we had 155,000 employees of the Dominion of Canada. On December 31, 1946, we had 174,000 employees, and instead of paying them $229,000,000 a year, as we did in 1946, we paid them $317,544,045.85-and don't forget the cents. I am bringing this up because I believe there are many people on the other side of the house with more brains than those sitting on the front benches.
So far as these controls are concerned this consolidation, Canada's fruit salad-for that is what it is-is all nonsense. Of course there has to be a certain measure of proper control. But why was not this consolidation printed
Emergency Powers

in French for the benefit of the French members? I should be very sore if I spoke good French and a copy of it were not available in French. How can the government expect to keep down the cost of living when it increases the number of its employees to the point where we are now paying them 8317,000,000 a year? It is the same old story; the higher she rises the harder she falls.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I suggest again that this section stand. It is necessary that it stand anyway until we finish the schedule. I do not think we shall make very much progress if we make general speeches in perpetuity on this section.
If the section is to stand, may I suggest that we be allowed to consider the schedule before we consider the other sections of the bill?

speechtext: Why?

Because there may be comments on other sections which would be influenced by the schedule. In any event it would assist us. There are amendments to make to the schedule. Many members have amendments to suggest, and if we knew where we stood with regard to the schedule it might speed up discussion on the remaining sections of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If that is the wish of the committee it is satisfactory to me. I thought we should go through the other sections first, but if anyone thinks there is any advantage in dealing with the schedule first, perhaps they should express themselves.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Any of us who have done any preparation had in mind that we would be proceeding with the other sections first before dealing with the schedule, as the minister indicated last night.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right. I stated explicitly last night the order which would be followed, that we would take section 1, let section 2 stand, and then take sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. I think we might as well do it in that way.

Would the minister not consider the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Kamloops? It is true that the schedule is more directly related to section 2 than to the later sections, but in these later sections there are provisions which may require amendment in the light of amendments that may be made to the schedule. I would urge on the minister that the reasons why it

is more convenient to consider the schedule before dealing finally with section 2 apply in greater or less degree to the other sections. speechtext: It is a matter of indifference to me. I am prepared to meet the wishes of the committee. I do not know just what my hon. friend has in mind though. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am also making objection on behalf of other members who are not here but are attending committees at this moment. On section 3-Employment of necessary persons.

On section 3, with respect, it seems to me that the time has arrived when some steps should be taken to have the civil service commission deal with the employees and staffs of the various boards operating under the authority of the orders enumerated in the schedule. Although there has previously been some discussion on some phases of this matter, there has been no comprehensive statement of the reason why it has been necessary over a lengthy period of time, in some cases going back to 1939 and in other cases to 1941, to have a body of employees outside the scope of the civil service commission in their manner of appointment, in their remuneration and in other provisions which are dealt with on a different basis from that of the civil service. I do not know what the minister is going to say with respect to the temporary features of the bill, but it seems to me that, if some demobilization is in contemplation with respect to the staffs, the time has come when a statement should be made by the ministry as to its intention with respect to the continuation outside the scope of the civil service of staffs of government boards.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The staffs of these boards were selected by the boards themselves, subject to the approval of the governor in council, because that seemed the only way in which they could be staffed. I remember the fall of 1941 when price ceilings were imposed and when it was thought it might be necessary to staff the wartime prices and trade board with some thousands of employees. About that time Mr. Gordon was appointed chairman of the board; he surrounded himself with some trusted associates, and they in turn got together a staff for the board as best they could. They had to move with great rapidity; they had to be in a position to give assurance to the people whom they took on. Many of these were taken on without remuneration, some of them with remuneration and so on. If the selection of these officials had been made by the civil service commission it would have been found that the rules established for the manning of the permanent service of Canada would have been entirely inappropriate. Therefore, after careful discussion, it was decided that the only practicable way of dealing with the matter was by authorizing the appointment of officials and staffs by the board itself, sublet to the approval of the governor in
council. The same thing was done in several other departments. I am satisfied that that wag the proper method to pursue.
At the present time, to try to bring the remaining employees of the wartime prices and trade board under the civil service commission, to have them selected by the civil service commission, appointed pursuant to the provisions of the Civil Service Act, would, in my opinion, be a most unwise thing to do. There would be a great deal of wasted effort, a great deal of confusion, and all unnecessary because it is anticipated that the staff of an organization such as the wartime prices and trade board will from now on be diminishing; perhaps in a few months from now it will be diminishing fairly rapidly. The system under which we are now operating should be allowed to run its course instead of a new system being instituted at this time in a late stage of the board's existence. The same question came up with regard to employees of the wheat board where the same arguments did not apply, but I think the house was convinced after a while that it was desirable that the employees of the wheat board be selected in accordance with the present system instead of by the civil service commission. But there is a much stronger reason why they should be continued under the present system in the case of the wartime prices and trade board and similar organizations, and it is this: these organizations before too long will be passing out of existence.

Supporting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, may I say that during the Easter recess the people in my constituency *who spoke to me were greatly concerned about the rising cost of living and the possibility of finding themselves with their dollar buying a great deal less as the months go by. Again and again people said to me, "Why is it that, now that the war is over and our people are home, we have to accept a situation where we have less milk, less butter, less foodstuffs?" We have to say frankly that the matter has not had full and frank discussion in parliament. I think the amendment moved by my deskmate places the matter in the hands of parliament. I cannot see the difficulty envisioned by the Minister of Justice in this matter. The amendment provides that the orders in council under the heading "wartime prices and trade board" shall not be revoked except by parliament. The purpose of these orders in council was to provide that prices should not rise beyond a certain level or get out of hand. If there is no pressure for the raising of prices, no emergency can exist and the orders themselves provide for keeping prices stable. Therefore I cannot see that the minister, if he accepts this amendment, is accepting anything which might result in a dangerous situation. It is perfectly democratic. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I went off on a tangent. It was an aside. I said I was not then talking about constitutional validity, and then I proceeded to talk about it, foolishly. What I was saying was that it becomes harder and harder every day to maintain an effective price control system in Canada. I want my hon.

friends in the C.C.F. to understand that. Some of them have not had executive or business experience. I do not say this unkindly at all, but some of them have not had that experience. The thing here is that a high type of executive experience and ability is required to operate a price control system. We had a great many able people on the staff of the wartime prices and trade board during the war years. Now a great number of those people have gone home. It must be borne in mind that they are pounded by the opposition every day in this house for being bureaucrats, and so on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do not pay any attention to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are subjected to that tirade of abuse in this house. Many people do not enjoy that. They get tired of it after a while; they say, "Why should I have to take that sort of thing?" and they go home. They also feel that the war emergency is passing and that they must go back and make provision for their own futures. For one reason and another we are losing and keep losing our good men all the time. That makes it very difficult to do these things. If you have a badly enforced price control system; if you have a system that you simply cannot enforce because the patriotic urge of the people is not as great as it was, because the selfishness of a good many people is a little more assertive than it is in time of war, there comes a time when it is better to have no control at all, apart altogether from the constitutional objection. Then of course, as conditions of supply and demand change, as scarcities disappear, it may be apparent that prices will move to higher levels and stay there for quite a while, if not indefinitely. Then a stage is arrived at when the dominion government should get out of price control. It may possibly be that w^e are decontrolling too rapidly. The Progressive Conservatives accuse us of decontrolling too slowly and urge us to be more rapid about it. The C.C.F. say that we are decontrolling too rapidly and that we should be slower about it. We are in a difficult position. Of course we cannot suit opposition parties. There is no use in trying to do that. We should be foolish to try it. We are taking a middle course, what we think is the sensible course; and we can discount quite a lot of what is said by opposition parties, I suppose, as being said for political purposes. Nevertheless, I think the original idea of this bill was the correct one, and that was to maintain the power to control in the agencies that are set up, and to continue it for a time and to leave it with the government to revoke these orders when the time comes

that they think these orders should be revoked. It would alter our plans very much if we froze a control system on the country for a year; and I do not think we should do so at the present time.

I do not rise to take issue with the Minister of Justice as to the constitutionality of the procedure, 'because I realize I am not learned in that respect. I believe, however, that the remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, have covered the subject fully. He has pointed out that if it is constitutional for us to have these controls at the present time, then surely under the measure before us it would be all right to have them for the remainder of the year or until parliament is called to attend another session.
Nor do I rise at this time to take part in the debate in answer to the remark of the right hon. gentleman to the effect that some of us in this group do not have the so-called necessary business experience properly to realize what is involved. I would say to him, however, that while some of us may not have had the opportunity to sit in control of big business, nevertheless we have all had the experience of running our own business. And let me say that if we had not paid more attention to the running of our own business than have some people I know of, then we would not have got very far with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With regard to my reference to business experience, I never ran a business, myself; and I do not think I am reflecting adversely on any person when I say he has not had business experience. Indeed I believe some of the best people in the country are those who have not had business experience. But what I have said is that one requires business experience in this kind of thing, and a lot of it.

Possibly on this occasion the right hon. gentleman and I are on an equal footing. The right hon. gentleman need not take a back seat to anyone, when it comes to a matter of applying common sense. I believe that during wartime, while he was in charge of an important department of government, he rendered a distinct service to the nation. Yet he did not have what some people would call the necessary business experience.
However, as I said, I did not rise to give advice which some people believe can come properly only from certain people. But I would say to the right hon. gentleman that when at times we speak emphatically, we are endeavouring to convey to him and to his colleagues the voice of the people back home,
and we believe that is something which requires more attention than it sometimes receives. When the right hon. gentleman suggested that during the course of debate some may at times be influenced by political reasons, let me point out to him that in this instance, if he does not heed with alarm the voice of the people with respect to the situation which is developing-and not gradually; but rapidly-in this country, then there will be more people who will have to pay attention to their political fences. Otherwise it will be bad for them. And let me say it will not happen to those in this part of the house. In my view this question has split right across party lines of every party in the house, with the exception of the C.C.E. This group has consistently pointed out to the government that the people are alarmed by the development of this situation.
However, when I rose it was my intention to state to the minister that I have been amazed to note his hesitancy-and I could have used a stronger word-in connection with the amendment offered, and to note that without very much consideration he was not prepared to accept the amendment offered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. As was pointed out by the hon. member, the adoption of the amendment would not prevent the wartime prices and trade board from easing off or, as he put it, from chiseling off some of the controls. Nevertheless the people of the country would be assured that the entire system of controls would not be done away with at least until parliament had been consulted in another session.
The minister appears before the committee with a bill which has within it more than fifty orders in council which, as he has said-and we all know-were in operation during past years. He says the time has now come when he wishes no longer to carry on these rules and regulations by orders in council, but wants to do it by statutory means.
I submit to him that the parliament which puts the stamp of approval on the bill should be the only body properly qualified to take that stamp of approval away. 1 submit that the amendment is a perfectly good one and is worthy of the minister's consideration, on that aspect alone. If we do place our stamp of approval on the bill, then surely no order in council should have the effect of wiping out a statute.

Mr. Chairman, this is a matter deserving of serious consideration by all members in the house. I believe what the minister has said is true, that the members of the wartime prices and trade board are weary.

However I do not think they have ever taken seriously criticism such as that which has been registered by the Tories. I do not think anyone takes it seriously. Sometimes I think not only are they something out of this world, but they are something out of this century. They are living in the world of a hundred years ago.
You are out of your head.

There have been some on the government's side of the house who apparently have been awake in the past fifty years, and who have realized that at least to some extent we have to protect the consumer. That right has been given under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act.
In spite of what my hon. friends say, we should consider the needs of the consumer. I believe the government's policy is based on the assumption that if we institute decontrol as consumer goods become more plentiful, prices will automatically adjust themselves. Since we began the process of decontrol we have not received enough literature on the subject to know just what the situation is. However, in the United States, where they have had a longer time in which to test the process of decontrol, they have found that this is not true. I would refer hon. members to Time magazine of April 7, and particularly to the page dealing with business and finance, to show what their experience has been. On page 43, under "Prices", there is a paragraph entitled, "Highest climb", which reads:
The magazine Mill dc Factory polled business men, found that forty-four per cent thought prices were too high. But only fifteen per cent expected to reduce them by summer. In a nationwide survey, the Wall Street Journal found that virtually no one is going to reduce them now.
Everybody wants the other fellow to reduce them but the individual manufacturer is not going to do anything about his own profits.
Profits in many industries were so fat, despite slackening sales, that few were being scared into price cutting.
And the last paragraph reads:
But out of fear, or the reluctance of most business men to charge less than the traffic would bear, there seemed to be small hope of general price reductions until a drastic drop in buying power forced them. Everyone was content to let George do it. And the longer prices remained unreasonably high, the farther-and faster-they would fall when the inevitable drop came.
I think that is a fairly good summary of the experience *mder decontrol in the United States. Here is another quotable quote from

the issue of April 14. This article refers to Quebec in our own country. This reads:
In a special dispatch from Quebec the Times talked about the "enormous profits" Canadian paper companies were making, showed that net profits of New York's International Paper Company had risen 270 per cent since 1943, that profits of another company had risen 500 per cent. But the price of newsprint was boosted again last fortnight.
Greatly perturbed by all this, Macy's president, Jack Straus warned in full-page ads last week: "Unless prices were lowered, we believe that a business recession is probable." But Macy's itself made no broad price cuts in cost of living items. Ironically, retailers and manufacturers were clinging to high profits as a hedge against the recession which they feared high prices would bring.
Are we to sit here and allow the manufacturers to drag us into a depression because we do not like to go to the trouble of controlling prices? Are we going to permit this thing to go on until consumer resistance and the lack of purchasing power bring on strikes and another depression? Sometimes when I read the opinions of some of our economists I think it is time that we started a new school of economics. They regard what they call the law of supply and demand as being something like the law of gravity, something over which they have no control. In this issue of Time someone has charted business booms and depressions, and to me it just looks like the records of smallpox which we used to consider were an act of God and that we could do nothing to prevent that disease. We used to think that all we could do was to record the death rate. Then some revolutionary in the field of medicine decided that we should not just record the death rate, that we should do something about the matter. If this parliament sits here like a bunch of nitwits and does nothing, then they are crazy.

The Minister of Justice did not press the constitutional question, but I gathered that he had in mind the problem of public opinion. He mentioned, when speaking earlier in the debate, that if we had not had the wartime prices and trade board during the war we would not have had an equitable system of distribution. One of the Tory members questioned that. Since he comes from the city of Toronto he may be able to look after his constituents in that area; but, coming from a rural constituency as I do, I realize the problems we would have been up against with no control over distribution. The first two orders in council which are dealt with in the bill do touch agriculture, and were based on the
recommendation of myself as Minister of Agriculture. They have to do with the subsidies which are paid on agricultural products. Some of these subsidies which are paid on products such as butter and others which are sold from time to time to ships that come into our ports, 'and which go out as ships stores, are collected by the person who supplies the commodities to those who are to utilize them. That is done for the purpose of making certain that the subsidies which are paid on those products are not provided by the treasury. In some cases it corresponds with the subsidies paid by the British, for example, on cheese. The British now pay the subsidy on cheese but we pay the subsidy on the milk which entered into the cheese. The British agreed to pay the subsidy on cheese which goes to Britain, but the Canadian government pays the subsidy on the cheese which is consumed in Canada. It was thought advisable to collect a subsidy on any commodities which were sold to ships which were supplied in Canadian ports from those who provided the commodity to the ships. These orders in council are to deal only with comparatively small quantities of the total product which is sold.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, I would say that I hope he will not insist on carrying into effect the last remark which he made. I am sorry I cannot be any more specific than that. It may be made within the next week or some time shortly, certainly before May 1. My understanding is that it will be made to apply as of May 1. The advisory committee which is composed of representatives from each of the departments of agriculture of the nine provinces and seven representatives from the federation of agriculture is meeting in Ottawa at the present time. They met yesterday, the day before, and they are meeting today. They are making recommendations as to what they think these price levels ought to be. I am sorry that I am not able to go farther than I did yesterday. I know I have the support of all members of the government in what I am about to say now. I spent my Easter holiday rambling around Ontario and I should like to talk about the Ontario farmers for a moment. I find that what the hon. member for Fraser Valley said is true not only of British Columbia but of Ontario. I found the farmers in Ontario cancelling orders for baby chicks, and they told me that the hatcheries were gassing baby chicks because of cancelled orders as a

result of increases in feed prices. I have no way of knowing whether the dealers know about the minister's ruling, but private enterprise is going ahead and raising the cost of feed all over Ontario. That is what the men on the farms tell me. Anyway, this is a serious matter because it will be reflected in the egg contracts with Great Britain. If we put the egg producer out of business, and if the cost of feed is sneaked up by the dealer and we pay no attention to it, we know what the resuit will be. If the hon. member for "Vancouver North has anything to say about double-talk, I can assure him that others than tire C.C.F. indulge in double-talk. Here we have a dual system of control, namely, price control on long-term contracts, price control of wheat, beef, pork, cheese and eggs, ami at the same time decontrol of all costs that go into production. This double-talk will be reflected in the farmers not being able to deliver eggs, cheese and meat, and it will result in a very bad condition and all kinds of dislocation.
V. ou cannot control the price which the farmer receives and then decontrol all costs, and yet that is the sort of double dealing the government is carrying on at the moment. Whether it intends to or not, that is the effect.
Not only should we review the whole question of subsidies, but we should go over all the subsidies and pay particular attention to those that have to do with production and the health of the nation. I do not care whether it comes under agriculture or public health, the subsidies that have to deal with the whole field of milk need overhauling. We should begin to reimpose these subsidies. Whether it is done in the name of public health or under agriculture I do not care, but the health of the Canadian people demands that we keep milk plentiful and reasonably cheap.

I should like to support the contention of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. We do not raise as many chicks in the district I come from but they lay more eggs per bird. I am getting letters from dozens of poultrymen and they tell me that the prices of the things that go into production have been raised, as the hon. member for Fraser Valley says. speechtext:
I want to say a word or two now with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. There is no double dealing or misunderstanding on the question of feed costs for chickens. One of the ingredients of feed for chickens is wheat, and a month or so ago we had a discussion in which everyone acknowledged that the price of feed for chickens had gone up because thirty cents a bushel had been added to wheat costs as a result of the action we took in order to change a condition, which everyone had previously criticized, of allowing wheat to be supplied at cost to the consumers over Canada at 774 cents for certain purposes. It was acknowledged by everyone that, as a consequence of that change, the cost of feed into which wheat entered for chickens and live stock of all kinds would go up by thirty cents.
There has been no double-talk about that at all. Everyone understood that, and two or three members in this house raised considerable criticism of it. We had discussions of the question and finally agreed that certain things should be done. One thing that was done was the very thing it is now suggested ought to be done, if we are to do it for others. We took the ceiling price off eggs. There is no control now on the height to which eggs can rise in Canada. They can go to any price. It is true they have not gone up much, probably not at all, but this is the season of the year in which they do not go up. They may go up later in the season; I am not in a position to say whether they will. At any rate, there is no ceiling on them. There is a ceiling on the grain that is fed. How long we are going to maintain that may be another question, but at the moment there is a ceiling. There has been no misunderstanding about that and some people have said that they will quit raising chickens because of that increase.
On the other question, I do not think this is the time at which we can discuss it and get anywhere by discussion. When the proposals are being made to change the position in relation to the whole situation we can discuss it, but this has to do with only one question:	Are we to collect subsidies
from the agencies that supply the farm commodity to those who are supplied, or ships and others, or are we to take it out of the treasury and pay it? Our practice has been to collect it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is just one remark I should like to make before the discussion proceeds, and it is to make reference to the statement made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley with regard to the price of feed.
The announcement made with regard to oats and barley, which I have checked since the discussion which took place before recess, did make this change in the price levels, that the new price levels are not the ceiling prices but the floor prices. There is a floor price guaranteed on barley of ninety cents and a floor price guaranteed on oats of 614 cents, basis No. 1 feed. The old guarantee was on the basis of No. 3 CW barley and No. 2 CW oats.
The result of that is that the new ceiling, which can be three cents higher than the floor on barley, and 34 cents on oats, is brought about by the fact that the basis now is No. 1 feed barley and the variation between No. 1 feed and No. 3 CW is about three cents, and on oats about 34 cents. So that there could be an increase, and there actually is an increase as a result of what is happening on the market. All the feed barley is selling at the ceiling. All grades of barley are selling at ninety-three cents, and they are entering into the production of the new feed mix, which would mean that if there were nothing else but the barley entering into the increase in price there might be an increase of about $1.20. There may be some other costs along the way which would be increased by the same percentage.
On oats there was an increase from a ceiling of 614 cents to a ceiling of possibly sixty-five cents. That allows for some increase on any oats that are in. The increase I referred to with regard to wheat applies. So that there could be an increase of somewhere between $1.20 and probably the $2 that was mentioned. We would have to know what the entire mix is before being able to estimate what that increase might be. That is due to the fact that the basis is now No. 1 feed instead of No. 2 CW, which allows a margin of three cents, or a margin of between ninety and ninety-three cents, within which the trade can carry on, and buy and sell barley. So that there is a possibility of an increase there.
I wanted to give that explanation before the discussion continued.

First of all, I wish to make very clear where I got my information from. It came from last year's president of the Pacific Coast Poultry Producers' Association. And just so that there may be no misunderstanding, I want to state the names of the officers this year. As I said before, eighty-five per cent of the eggs produced in British Columbia are produced in the ridings of New Westminster and Fraser Valley.
This year's president is J. 0. Bowles. The past president was Gordon Billingsley. The vice-president is Francis Parker, and the secretary is Mr. Headey. I want to have those names on record, just to show that the figures came from responsible people, people who represent eighty-five per cent of the poultry producers of British Columbia. That is an important point.
Another point I wish to make clear to my hon. friends from Saskatchewan particularly is that the people of Fraser Valley are in no way objecting to an increase in the price of grain. That is perfectly clear. But what we do object to is an increase in the cost of feed to our farmers. However we do not object to the people in Saskatchewan getting more.
Second, and most important, the people of Fraser Valley are not opposed to controls. I made myself clear on that the other day. The only action of the government so far to which we object is that they have taken controls off too rapidly, and have taken them off some things from which they should not have taken them. I believe that before we are through, if we are to prevent inflation we shall put back many of the controls we have taken off. I believe the people I represent are in favour of that. I have had absolutely no objection from anyone in my riding to the fact that we have had controls; but I have had a lot of objections from a few prominent individuals-and they do not bother me much, because they know they are well represented-to any controls being taken off. I want that point made clear.
When I came first to the House of Commons I told the people of my riding that I was not going to be a back-bencher. And in this connection I pay my respects to the new member. When I first arrived in the House of Commons, I returned after the session to my people and said I was not a back-bencher. I had the seat that the hon. member now occupies, and I told them I might as well have been in a chicken-house in Chilliwack, because I could neither hear nor see from my seat. I hope the hon. member will be moved up to a better seat before long. It is no good down there, I can assure him.
I shall quote some figures, to show the minister's department that if they would come to the proper source for information they would get correct figures, and have them available. In 1946, in the province of British

I am not allowed to refer to them, but I imagine they will get their increase. This is only the chance I shall have, so that I am going to cover a few other things I represent a dairying district as well as a poultry producing district. This is the only opportunity that the dairy producers will have to put their case before the house. Again I want to give the authority for the figures I am using. He found that it cost 58-7 cents last year to produce a pound of butter fat, with nothing allowed for labour. These farms are based on an average value of S21,269; the average value per acre being $179 and ranging from $215 to S143. I am going to pass on because I want to cover berries. Everything goes into the production cost in Fraser Valley. I have just come back from that district. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is not in his seat at the moment but I hope his parliamentary assistant can tell us something about these tons and tons and carloads of nails that are going to British Columbia. I made it a point to go to every store in my riding. One store had a full keg of something that would be very handy for putting on shiplap to repair an old building, a keg of three and a half inch spikes. Another store had some boot nails-I have one here-at sixty cents a pound, which could be used to repair a building. Another rather big store had some copper nails two and a half inches in size at sixty cents a pound. I have never seen copper nails before. If you weigh them you find that it comes to exactly one-half cent per nail. That may be all right for the farmers in Ontario where you have all the millionaires and where they do not care about the cost of producing farm products. The Ontario federation of agriculture did not make any complaint anyway. Maybe they can afford to pay sixty cents a pound for nails to repair a coop, but we cannot afford to pay it in Fraser Valley or in any other part of British Columbia.

I will back you up? The hon. member for Qu'Appelle paid me a little compliment this afternoon. I will put it another way. I will be glad to have the hon. member cooperate with me in any
way possible. I do not know what you need nails for in Peterborough anyway with all the manufacturers you have there.
I want to deal now with berries. I come from a wonderful riding. I am very proud of the riding I represent. We produce about half the berries that are used in the entire Dominion of Canada.
It is the berries.

I just want to give certain figures of the berries we produced last year. I am naturally modest about Fraser Valley and I hesitate to mention it at any time, but last year we produced 4,863,683 pounds of strawberries and 11,475,428 pounds of raspberries.
