I knew if I waited long enough Kamloops would ask for it and he will get it in a minute. In the meantime I have other more important matters to speak of. I wish to point out to the prairie farmers that we were able to ship only 90,000 crates of strawberries last year to the prairie provinces, our great market. We want to ship there at a fair price, but unfortunately last year we could ship only 90,000 crates. I will come to Kamloops in a minute. I am no socialist by any manner or means; I am a capitalist. Two other fellows and I own a farm; they own the most part and I own the rest. I do not believe in socialism; I believe in free enterprise. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when he said that this government and no other government dare take off these controls, but they are taking them off bit by bit and we see the profits that are being made as quoted by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar yesterday and as quoted in the Star today. The United States is admitting that they cannot control prices at the present time.
That is under the free enterprise you believe in.

We can improve free enterprise but never socialism. I have been trying to improve the hon. member for Kamloops but have not succeeded yet; you cannot improve the impossible. I will tell you why we shipped only 90,000 crates to the prairies last year. I was successful in moving the adjournment of the house to discuss the shortage of containers. One of these downtrodden lumber operators in British Columbia could not pay fifteen cents an hour wage

Emergency Powers
increase, but they can make a profit in their business in spite of strikes. One gentleman who did not know one end of a board from another came from Toronto and took over a sawmill with watered stock that showed a profit of over $400,000 in a few months. In my opinion, that same group of operators from Toronto, headed by this notorious brewer who has now moved into British Columbia's lumber business, are doing everything they can to prevent us from getting crates this year by fomenting trouble with the honest loggers in British Columbia. If something is not done about the matter, I shall be moving more adjournments of the house and I hope to have the support of my hon. friends opposite.
The Minister of Agriculture has given me one assurance. I do not want to put words into his mouth, but I understood him to say that when the subsidy is taken off butter the price will not be less than it is now. I should like him to repeat that. That is correct?
I want these controls to be more effective. I want some controls to be restored. I do not think you can ask the dairy producers to go on producing forever at present prices when you permit other industries to make the profits which have been quoted in this house and never denied, and when you permit the lumbermen of my own province of ' British Columbia to amass fortunes they have never had before. It will be pretty poor pickings for Cruickshank with the lumbermen at the next election, but that is all right with me. When they can make these profits our dairymen are not going to be satisfied with the present price of butter in British Columbia.
I turn to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, then next to the Minister of Labour, and I shall finish off with the hon. member for Kamloops. I did not take part in the debate on the address, but I believe that every member for British Columbia is dissatisfied with the deal made so far as veterans homes are concerned. I find that the minister's own officials have given him two different lists of figures. One sets out that it costs $169.50 to heat a house till the plaster is dry in a home in the sunny Fraser valley, and then a week iater the minister brings down a return saying that it costs $28.05. It is time that we put to work in the Department of Veterans Affairs some unemployed who can add and substract. The veterans of Fraser Valley are not asking for homes for nothing, but they are asking for a fair deal, and when any official at Ottawa tells me that it costs $184.95 to drain a veteran's home in the Chilliwack district I
liMr. Cruickshank.]
say that he does not know what he is talking about-$184.95 to drain an acre and a half of land in the Chilliwack district. This is in order, Mr. Chairman, because it all comes under these fifty-seven varieties.
I am not satisfied with the deal the Minister of Labour has given in the Tashme camp for Japs. If the truth were known it would make us blush.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Let us have the blushing.

You give me the facts and figures and you will do the blushing, or bring the figures before the public accounts committee and you will find who will do the blushing. I am a little bitter about Tashme when a farm, which never made a profit of $500 a year, in twenty years gets $500 a month rental over a period of years and can get waterworks and all the buildings when hospitals and schools cannot get these things and, in addition, get a cash settlement. I would ask the government to have inquiries made about Tashme camp.
So far as my riding is concerned, we will support this government's efforts to maintain controls 100 per cent and, if necessary, restore some of the controls that have been taken off, which we believe should not have been taken off. We believe that it is in the best interests of our district and of Canada as a whole that controls be maintained. I believe that everyone in British Columbia has that opinion. I have never heard one request that controls be removed other than from Toronto and Kamloops. Kamloops is not a bad town to get out of.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I shall support the C.C.F. amendment. I believe it is the fairest one to date in connection with controls, unless the government brings down something better.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend's remarks about Tashme camp, let me say that it is all very well for one who has no responsibility as an administrator to bandy these things about, but if my hon. friend has anything he has a duty to perform. Let him bring the facts before the public accounts committee and he will not need to worry about the labour department coming out in the clear. It is the easiest thing in the world to make statements of the kind he has made. If he thinks there is anything wrong let him bring the matter before the public accounts committee and let us get the truth.

Nobody should
know better than the present minister how easy it is to get up and bandy something around without any responsibility.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the discussion continues, may I remind the committee that we are dealing with order in council 6759. This afternoon there was considerable discussion on eggs, the cost of producing eggs and the return the farmer received for producing them, but upon reading order in council 6759 I find no mention of eggs. If hon. members will look at the second and third preambles they will see that they read as follows:
And whereas the subsidy in respect of creamery butter, cheddar cheese, concentrated whole milk products, white beans and yellow eye beans is now being paid through the Department of Agriculture;
And whereas it is deemed necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada to provide for the repayment of subsidy involved in such goods . . .
That is to say, the goods mentioned in the second preamble. It will be noticed that section 2 of the regulations reads as follows:
(b) "subsidized goods" means creamery butter, cheddar cheese, concentrated whole milk products, white beans or yellow eye beans, or such other goods as may be designated by order of the Deputy Minister ot Agriculture by notice in Canadian war orders and regulations.
I mention these things to remind hon. members that this order in council does not refer to eggs in. any way; it refers only to the subsidy on dairy products and certain beans, which subsidy must be repaid to the government when these goods are exported. I do not wish to curtail discussion, but I believe that the committee would like to deal with the contents of the order in council and not have too wide discussion.

In connection with eggs, I should like to quote two or three sentences from a letter which I have received. I think I am in order because some of these people also produce milk and butter, and depend very much on the price of eggs-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think it would be fair to interrupt the hon. member for Kootenay West at this time; but would it be agreeable to the committee that, afer he makes his statement in regard to eggs, we discuss the contents of the present order in council?

For the information of the committee, I shall quote from a letter written by Mr. Godfredsen, president of the Kootenay Cooperative Poultry Association, and dated March 18, 1947. He is one of the largest poultrymen in the district and is a responsible and practical man. He writes as follows:
Dear Mr. Herridge
I am very much surprised of the announcement over the radio that the ceiling price was taken of eggs, if that is to compensate the
poultry farmer for the increase in feed price, it is absolutely inadequate as we can only get ceiling price three month of year.
Toward the end of his letter he says:
Coming back to feed prices wheat is eleven dollars more a ton and laying mash is five dollars more a ton and it was announced over the radio that barley and oats would go up too if that is the case laying mash will be still higher.
In addition to that, I have a letter from Mr. Charles E. Tutt, secretary of the same association, who is a poultryman and a responsible person. In this letter he says:
We heartily endorse a greater return to the Canadian wheat producers, but we strongly resent the fact that a rise in the price of feed wheat directly discriminates againat the poultry-men.
In his letter he mentions the fact that at the present time there is a surplus of eggs which cannot be sold, on the local market. These are No. 1 eggs and they were sold to the Swift Canadian Company at Nelson for twenty-three cents a dozen. He also mentions that the cost of feed and so forth nullifies the floor price which has been placed under eggs in the British contract. I urge the minister to have this situation investigated.

What subsidies are now being paid on goods classified as subsidized goods, namely, creamery butter, cheddar cheese, concentrated whole milk products, white and yellow beans? How many of these subsidies have the government already announced will be withdrawn, and on what dates will they be withdrawn?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
As I said before recess, the government has under consideration the whole matter of returns on dairy products which is largely the items covered in the order in council that we are now discussing. There are smaller items such as beans which enter into it, but most of it is dairy products. The position with regard to these is pretty generally understood in the committee. We did pay and are still paying a ten-cent subsidy on butter fat; we are also paying a subsidy of thirty cents on milk which enters into cheese, and we are paying a subsidy on milk which enters into the production of canned milk of different kinds.
The question which is now under consideration is as to whether these subsidies should be taken into the price. If they are they will probably be taken into the price very shortly, within a few days time. This particular order in council gives the government authority to deal only with subsidies on exports such as ships' supplies, until that time is reached. In other words, we are spending a lot of time in
Emergency Powers

talking about something that may last for only ten days. After that, it will be necessary to have the order because of these other items, provided that subsidies on dairy products are done away with and the whole matter is put into the price. It will probably be only a short time until the announcement is made. I have said on two or three occasion that any changes which do take place will take place on May 1. The whole matter is under consideration. The matter that has been discussed during the greater part of the time that we have had these orders before the committee is the question of increased cost of feed. That question is being fully considered by the advisory committee which is now sitting, and it will be fully considered by the government when the recommendations are made by that committee to the government. In other words, the government will not reach a decision on what should be done with regard to butter, cheese, milk and even eggs, which do not come under this at all, without having before them all the implications of the increases in feed costs. They will also have under consideration all the implications of the increases which have already been made since there was any previous increase in the cost of grain, increases which have already been made in the returns for farm products, and within a few days time with regard to almost everything that is covered by this order in council an announcement will be made which will probably do away with the greater part of the necessity for it.
I would suggest that I think we can discuss most of the questions which are being asked better when my estimates are before the house, which, may be coming up on Friday evening and the following Friday evening as usual. At least by the second Friday evening we shall probably have all the facts in front of us and we shall be able to discuss the matter to much better advantage then than we can now.
From what the minister says one could almost draw the inference that subsidies are to disappear. AVould the committee be right in understanding that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Well, I have come as close to saying that as I could. I rather think so.

Probably a hint is as good as a nod to a blind farmer. Will the minister give consideration to lifting the ceiling price also on dairy products and on bacon products? I was interested in what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said this afternoon, indicating that there is something wrong. The planned economy which those to the left would like 
and the planned economy which we have had on the right has caused confusion such as agriculture has never known before in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On that side of the house.
The minister is not a farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was on a farm.
Yes, but the minister left it pretty early. Had, he stayed there he would have realized the position the farmers are in today.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They are in the best position they ever were.

Why is it you are falling down on the egg contract to Britain; why on the cheese contract; why on the butter contract? Why have you fallen down on the bacon contract, and why have you made the most nonsensical wheat contract the world has ever known? So that agriculture has not a great deal of confidence and does not know where we are going.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Did you vote for it?
No, I did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You were not in the house.

Surely the time has come, in view of the political confusion that has been caused by this type of state panic, when the minister should give some consideration to removing the ceilings, and admit that, so far as agriculture is concerned, they have been a deterrent. I say to the ex-minister of finance as well that, so far as the wartime prices and trade board and fixed prices are concerned, the farmer has been the guinea pig in the whole picture. He has been the guinea pig of this new economic experiment. My hon. friends may laugh, but let them go up and down the side lines of the dominion and the people will tell them, and more vociferously than I am doing, and not in parliamentary language either.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have seen ten times as much of the dominion and of every province as my hon. friend has seen. I have been through every province. He lives in Toronto and Ontario only. Let him go and see the great west.
I have been west too, but if my hon. friend has gone all over the map in the short time that he has done I can understand why he has seen so little of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You have a localized viewpoint; that is all.

Emergency Powers
I remember when members of the present cabinet were on this side. They did not see as much of the back concessions as they thought they did.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: What did the farmer get then?

He got a fairer share of the world market than you have given him. He got a fairer share of it than you are giving him now. It is all very well to talk about 1930 and 1931, but I have sat here longer than the Minister of Agriculture and I say to him that no one can tell me that the farmer did not get a fairer share of world markets than he gets today.
At what prices?
If the hon. gentleman expects to be big enough to run all the industries of Canada he should know more than he does.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You should know more about it.
I do, and I know this-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Nothing whatever.
Bring on the cheering section when you can't take it.
I am not disturbed by little Chicago over here, or over there either.
When the hon. gentleman was in power they were not getting any prices at all.
What did you sell your products at?
Starvation prices; that is all.
That is the most antiquated sort of defence that anyone can put up. I am not going to go back-
Oh, oh.

There are those, especially to my right, who would like to suggest that the depression came about because the Conservative party came into power at a time when we faced the greatest crisis in the history of the world. If my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. party has made a study of the situation; if he is big enough to take over all the industries of Canada, he ought to know more about what caused the depression in 1929 than he appears to know.
I say to my hon. friends from western Canada, and to some on my own side too perhaps-
Perhaps?
-what caused the depression in 1929 was-
Bennett.
The hon. member says "Bennett."
Well, "R. B." was a great fellow, but the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett was not in power from 1921 to 1930.
We had good times then.

You had good times, but more Canadians left this country than were brought in or were born in Canada, and the natural increase was lost. We lost a million people during those years, people who found better employment and a better opportunity in foreign countries than they could find at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why did he leave Canada?
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why did R. B. leave it?
He was sick of you.

I do not know, Mr. Chairman, but knowing what happened between 1921 and 1930, I presume the people who went away thought that some day again they would have to endure another Liberal government. In any event, Mr. Bennett has been accepted with good grace in another country and I do not think he is any discredit to Canada. He is a distinguished citizen where he is.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No one ever suggested otherwise.
Order.
My right hon. friend is a distinguished man, but I say to him I have no apologies to offer for Mr. Bennett.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Neither have I. I am a great friend of his.	.

He never recognized it very much, but I suppose you are. I can only say that, so far as agriculture in Canada is concerned, never in the history of this dominion has it been in the confusion it is in at the present time.
Oh, oh.
My hon. friend always says more sitting down than he can say standing up. He is always chiming in.

The farmers were never so well off as they are today.

Emergency Powers
My hon. friends may twit and make these empty gibes-
No gibe at all.

-but history will prove what I say to those who, running, may read. Those who run may read, but my hon. friend perhaps would rather sit than either run or read. May I say this to the committee, Mr. Chairman, and you need not take my word for it. The Minister of Agriculture and the right hon. gentleman who is leading the house have no doubt read the records of the Geneva conference on world economic affairs, and they no doubt know-it is now common history which every student of economics understands-that in this dominion the greatest contributing factor to the depression of 1929 was a clumsy effort to plan agriculture. I remember stepping out into the corridor on one occasion when I stated that Canada should have a balanced economy in which we would pay more attention to mixed farming instead of putting all our eggs in one basket-one wheat basket. I remember that at that time my hon. friends from the province of Quebec who were on the opposite side of the house used to refer to the fact that we were listening to nothing but wheat; and finally, as I remember well, one gentleman said to me, "You don't understand. We have the wheat market of the world in the palm of our hands. We are the bread-basket of the world and we can dictate prices."
Oh, oh.
I can quite understand why my hon. friend does not understand this. He does not listen long enough to learn anything.
What was the price of wheat then?

If you do not know that much, why enter into this discussion at all? We know that during 1925 and 1926 Italy and Czechoslovakia, France and Germany, every country in the world, all raised their tariffs, yes, higher than the price of our wheat. W'hy? Because, as reported at the world conference, they were fearful of the wheat pools of western Canada fixing a price and demanding that price, and were afraid of the monopoly. We have seen the results. We sold wheat at thirty-five cents a bushel.
The world did not suffer a depression because Bennett was elected in Canada and wheat was forty cents. The world did not say, "Because of that, we will put 29,000,000 men out of jobs". Anyone who talks that sort of thing is just talking stupid political nonsense. That worked all right for an election or two, but it is not according to the facts and the records

of history. Let us look the facts square in the face. The Minister of Agriculture knows now what the facts are. He says to my hon. friends to the left, "Leave your amendment; we are not sure whether we will adopt it or reject it. It may be all right. Let us look it over". The minister is the same as he has been for the last four years; he does not know whether he is going or coming.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You are certainly
going; that is one sure thing.
The Minister of Agriculture cannot tell me tonight why we have seen the greatest reduction in dairy' production that we have had in the last twenty-five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I can tell you what the reduction is, but you will not believe me.

I can tell you what it is and why7. I asked you this afternoon but you would not tell me. We have reduced our bacon production. You have not told the country that before your party came into power we sent more bacon to Britain than you sent this yrear. You have not told the people that. You have not told them that you made a contract with Britain for 350.000,000 pounds three years ago and fell down by 100,000,000 pounds, and revised the contract and made another for tw?o hundred and fifty-and by the signs of the times and the brood sows that are going to market you have not filled that.
The handwriting is on the wall, Mr. Chairman. The farmers of Canada today have lost confidence in the present government. They do not know what to sow. They are waiting for the Natural Products Marketing Act. They have read the Wheat Board Act. They do not know whether the Minister of Agriculture will tell them what they have to sow, where they are going to sell, how much they are going to get for their product, but they do know that they pay about three times as much today for a binder as they paid in the last great war which my hon. friends hark back to with regard to high prices. They know they pay about twice as much for farm labour as they paid then and that they get about half as much for their wheat. As to price ceilings, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said this afternoon that she believes they will be good things for all. But even a kindergarten class knows they are no good on one side unless they are operative on the other side. Personally I do not think they are any good on either side. I hope I do not embarrass the cabinet ministers, because I understand there has been division on this in the last five years. I do not believe that a farmer like the

Emergency Powers
Minister of Agriculture could sit in a cabinet like this without having embarrassed the ex-minister of finance; and I do not believe any old Scotch Presbyterian free economist like him could sit there and not feel that the whole show was being put out of commission. We have carried controls to the limit. We have carried controls to the point of detriment to our supply of products overseas. We have carried controls to the point that the peoples in Europe, hungry for food, are deprived of wheat which would have been produced in Canada. My right hon. friend tonight says. "What about the price of feeds to produce this bacon and meat products? Where does the feed come from?"

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Off the farm.

Yes, off the farm. I hope that some day in the cabinet you will tell the rest of your colleagues, the new found economists, why it is that for Britain, that we feel we want to help, the farmers of Canada are asked to send their wheat over at S200 million less than they can get at the world price for a year, and yet you make the British pay more for lumber than the people of Canada have to pay. Do you think it is fair for the farmers of Canada to lose $200 million on their product which they are exporting overseas and yet at the same time tell the lumbermen of British Columbia that they can charge the Britisher what they want to, even if he needs a house as badly as he needs bread. What type of economy is this?
We are not surprised at the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, in view of the fact that she is a member of the fairer sex. I think she is more sympathetic than any member of the cabinet when she says it is a planned economy, but it is only half-planned. It is a mixture, and so it is. It must be a mixture when the western farmer and wheat producer of Canada surrenders $200 million a year, but the lumberman of British Columbia can charge $123 a thousand for rough lumber for Britain.
How much do you get for pulp in Ontario?
Tell us about the price of lumber.
What is that?
How much do you get for pulp in Ontario?
Oh, you are usually fair.
We get as much and more for pulp than you would take to produce it.
You raised it $8 a ton.

Yes; and freight rates rose $3 a ton, and we raised wages in Montreal last week $3 a ton. May I inform you-and I think you are a great defender of the British Columbia lumberman; I have no brief for them-that if you want to talk about the pulp and paper industry, we in the pulp and paper industry have no apologies to make, despite the snipes that have been coming from various sides of this house.
You have been doing very well.
Yes; just as well as under your management.
Apparently a whole lot better.

If you could run them all together better than we can run them separately, you are a better wizard than you have ever indicated here in Ottawa. I will say this, in any event, for the benefit of my hon. friend from British Columbia because he is a free enterpriser-and I say it for the benefit of the leader of the C.C.F. party because he interrupted me: the great pulp and paper industry of Canada has been the greatest stabilizer, as the ex-minister of finance knows, of any industry in Canada. Half of that industry has been in bankruptcy for the last fifteen years. No industry in Canada pays its employees as high wages, and no industry in Canada has paid its shareholders less dividends. Those are facts which are irrefutable, and I challenge anyone to rise in the house tonight and say they are not right.
Watered stock.

Watered stock, you say. I could tell you about some of your companies but I might get too personal if I did. But those are the facts and they are undeniable; and today we are paying to labour the highest base rate paid by any industry in Canada. It is true that some will say, "You have had an increase in your commodity." So we have. Where is this venture capital to come from? \\ here is the capital to come from with which you are to take over all these industries? Will you get it for less than two per cent? The pulp and paper industry in Canada in the last fifteen years have not paid an average of two per cent on the venture capital which made it possible in Canada. I challenge my friends to say where they are going to get the money to take over all this industry at any less. Let us throw the cards down and see where we come in this new economy of
Emergency Powers

yours. Do you think you can run them all better than anybody runs them separately?
Address the chair.

I apologize to you, Mr. Chairman. I would much rather address you than address my hon. friend. I think you are both very fine, but if I were going to trust my estate to either, I would entrust it to you, Mr. Chairman.
I urge upon the Minister of Agriculture, and urge it upon him before it is too late-

What did you do under
Bennett?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I do not know what my hon. friend said. However, if you think you are contributing something to the debate, then you serve a purpose.

I am sure you are not,
anyway.

I cannot tell what my hon.
friend's interruptions are. If he would make them audible and make them clear, I might be able to deal with them, but I do not know what he said. I know he is saying something and I think he understands it probably as well as the rest of the house does.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, following what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said, I am not supporting her theory that we should have a planned economy, but I support her to this extent:	If you are going to have a
half planned economy you must have it all. You on the left and you on the right had better get together. You have a half planned economy now.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You have got none.

You have a bureaucracy built up on a planned economy. You do not want to go out and say you will leave it to the law of supply and demand. But I ask you now, do you think them is any other way of establishing agricultural production in Canada unless you give an incentive to the farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am going to talk
after you are through. Go right on.

I know pretty well what
the Minister of Agriculture will say, too. I realize that he will tell us about the low prices in 1932. I realize that he will tell about the Tory reactionaries. I know about the line he will take. If I gave it, he would be glib enough to find another one, probably, in another speech; so I am not going to relate it all. But I know very well that at least fifteen times I have heard the Minister
of Agriculture tell about the low prices in 1932 and what the farmers went through. That is an old, tottering and dusty argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
You don't like to hear
about it, do you?

I don't like to hear about it from a man who is a right honourable, who should know better, and does know better. I don't like him to use it for political purposes, when he knows it is not true. And after some years of activities we expect people to stick to the truth of things. You can't stand up tonight and tell us that the prices we received in, 1932 were due to the fact that it happened we changed governments in Canada in 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You have a bad conscience.
No, but I have to recall the type of argument you have put up for the last ten years in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You really think it is true.
I know it is not true, just as you know it is not true. Will you tell me if that is not true-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Chair, chair.

Mr. Chairman, Lam reminded that you are in the chair.
I say to the right hon. gentleman: When you rise tonight will you tell us why it was that when your party came into power in 1921-and, that is history-we had more live stock production, and sold more live stock products to Great Britain than we did grain? Will you tell us why it was that we were eating more bacon at that time than we are today. Will you tell us why it was that when you went out of power in 1930, before the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett and his party took office, we were importing New Zealand butter and Danish bacon? My hon. friend knows it. I have heard him use it in the house. We were eating Danish bacon in Canada; we were eating New Zealand butter in Canada in 1930 than we were exporting from Canada. We were importing more live stock production into Canada. But in 1921, about thirty years ago, we were selling, at those lower prices, $77 million worth of live stock products more than we are buying.
What happened in those years? The Danish farmers were taking grain from western Canada, feeding hogs and sending bacon back to sell in the butcher shops at Regina. Eighteen thousand head of cattle were impor-

Emergency Powers
ted in tin cans in 1930. We were eating canned beef in 1930, beef canned in the Argentine.
True, during the war, the bacon people had some exports; but it is rapidly falling off again. It has fallen from 350,000,000 pounds two or three years ago to 250,000,000 pounds now. And if you keep the price ceilings on those things we have to sell and take the price ceilings off those things we have to buy, then I shudder to think how much more we shall be falling down in, our supplying of the British market. And if we cannot supply it in a time of stress and strain, then we have no right to claim it in a time of peace and prosperity.
I urge the minister and ask him to urge the government to let go of these bureaucratic controls. You cannot control them all unless you are going to do it with machine-guns. The farmers are paying today double the amount in wages they were paying back in 1921-and I know whereof I speak. We are selling our wheat and losing hundreds of millions of dollars a year on your fixed ceiling price. And your exports of other products are falling down. Even the British people are laughing at the mess you have made of Canadian agriculture.
I leave it to you: If you do not listen tonight to what I have said' you will hear from the farmers in the next election.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we opened the discussion this evening on two orders in council which have been in effect for some four years, and which will probably be in effect for some few weeks more at the most, I did not expect that for the third or fourth time during this session we were to have a full-dress debate on agriculture. Nor did I expect that it would carry on into all the activities of the government, or of all governments we have had during the century. But we have just listened to a speech which covers all that.
My hon. friend has just been making statements which are not borne out by the facts. He has tried to leave the impression that in years gone by there was at some time higher production and that there have been higher exports of products than we have had recently As a matter of fact we still have high production and exports. But I just wish to leave a few figures with him and with the committee in order to indicate how far from the facts he really is.
In 1930, a year which was spoken of, the production of cheese in Canada was 119,000,000 pounds. The production of cheese in 1942 was
208,000.000 pounds; in 1943 it was 167,000,000
pounds; in 1944 it was 182,000.000 pounds, and in 1945 it was 189,000,000 pounds. In 1946 it is true that it was down, as compared with these last few years, to 148,000,000 pounds. But that is still much higher than 119,000,000 pounds.
But that is not the most important figure. When we talk about parties going out of power, another party has gone out of power since that. That was the party led by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, which went out of power in 1935. The production of cheese in that year was 101,000,000 pounds. And from the time they came into office in 1930, when it was quite low-119,000,000 pounds-it still went on down. It went down during all the time they were in office, until it reached
101.000.	000 pounds.
He kept it up well in those hard times.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will not mislead the committee either.

The minister says he wishes to show the difference. I never mentioned one figure about production in 1930. Go back to 1921, and see if what I said was not true. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

Certainly.

Now, coming back to 1934, which was the lowest year-and 1935 was about the same. There was 100,000,000 pounds in 1934 and
101.000.	000 pounds in 1935. The government changed in that year, in the fall of 1935. In

1936 the production went up to 120,000,000 pounds; in 1937 it went up to 131,000,000 pounds; and by 1940, the first year of the war, it was up to 146,000,000 pounds. It went on up, under the present government, and under the agricultural policy that has been spoken about, to 206,000,000 pounds, which is the highest production of cheese in the present century.
Now, one might go on and deal with other products which have been spoken about. Let us take concentrated milk products. In 1932 it was 110,000,000 pounds. In 1935, the year the government of Mr. Bennett went out, it was 105,000,000 pounds. It was down. It had been down much lower in the intervening period, but it was down 5,000,000 pounds that year. It went up next year to 109,000,000 pounds; the next year to 137,000,000 pounds; next year to 157,000,000 pounds; the next year to 166,000,000 pounds; the next year to
193,000,000 pounds; the next- year to 236,000,000 pounds. To save reading a lot of figures, by 1946 it had got up to 302,000,000 pounds. There has not been any reduction in production over a period in connection with that.
The same kind of figures could be produced with regard to other items. Let us look at eggs for a moment. In 1930 our production was 250,000,000, but by 1935 the preceding government had succeeded in getting it down to 244,000,000. Since this government has been in, it has gone up from the first year of the war when it was 250,000,000 to 1945 when we got it up to 393,900,000. It has dropped down slightly in 1946.
What are you paying in subsidies?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The hon. member wants to know what we are paying in subsidies. I have heard nothing from the other side of the house but the suggestion that we ought to get rid of all these controls and special considerations we have in connection with these matters and let trade take its free course. That is a rather peculiar policy to hear from my hon. friends on the other side; nevertheless it is the kind of policy which has been spoken of. What was the position taken by our hon. friends back in 1929 when they were contesting an election back and forth across this country? It was that there was protection in every other country in the world. They said that they had protection in Germany, in France and in Italy; they said that there was no unemployment in those countries, that the only countries where there was unemployment were countries like Britain, Canada and other countries which followed the same policy as this country. They 
said, "Put us in power and we will blast our way into the markets of the world". They were blasting for five years, and by the end of that time they had created the situation indicated by these figures, not only with regard to agriculture but with regard to every other industry in the Dominion of Canada.
Now my hon. friend comes back and says that we have been in power for some time and that there is a certain situation existing with regard to agriculture. What is the situation? In 1946, in spite of the fact that production of hogs is down; in spite of the fact that production is down on some dairy products; in spite of the fact that production is down slightly on eggs as compared with the previous year, the highest net return the farmers of this country ever received was received in 1946. That means only one thing. If the production was down, then the return per unit must be very high as compared with the previous year. There is only one year in the history of this country when even the gross income from farm operations was higher than 1946, 'and that was in 1944.
The products which were sold in 1944 and which brought about the high gross income of that year were not products produced in 1944. One of the products which brought about a greater increase in gross farm cash returns in 1944 than any other was grain, and that grain which was sold in 1944 in such great quantities was not all grown in 1944. That grain was grown in 1942 and the years preceding, and in 1943. It was stored in our elevators and sold in 1944 and thus brought a considerable amount of cash into the pockets of the farmers of this country.
In spite of that, the cash income in 1944 was $1,849 million, whereas in 1946 the gross cash income was only $90 million less in spite of the fact that we were selling only the production of the year 1946 in the main. The net income of our farmers was the highest, whereas the gross income was only $90 million less than it was in the highest sales year that agriculture ever had in this country. We have increased the price of grain. My hon. friend wants to know why it was done. If he looks at the record he will find that there are only three provinces that had a lower gross return in 1946 as compared with 1944, and those were Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Why were those provinces down in gross return while the other provinces were not? The reason is obvious. Year by year we have been increasing the returns that can be obtained from every farm production that can be produced by the feeding of grain, but we have not increased the prices of feed grain

Emergency Poioers
since 1943 until this year. This year, in justice to the farmers who have been growing the feed that is being fed to live stock in surplus all over the Dominion of Canada, we have suggested that the prices ought to go up. If that increase does result in a slight increase per ton in the cost of the feed that is being fed to live stock, it will be found by the end of the first year for which statistics are available that it did not do anything more than give justice to the people who produce the grain that is being fed in surplus elsewhere.
What I want to suggest with regard to that is this:	The discussions which we have
had tonight clearly indicate that there are some men v'ho claim to be farmers but who have not followed the records in relation to % agricultural production, more particularly in relation to agricultural returns. There has been a constant upward levelling of prices over the returns from those products which are produced from the feeding of grain. There has not been a comparable increase in the price of grain itself to those farmers who grow the grain and who sell it to those who are going to feed it. The reason for the announcement that has been made is partly to adjust that situation. When it is adjusted, when we get our returns, if we have anything like an average crop year in 1947 it will be found once more that the three prairie provinces which produce grain occupy a position in relation to both gross and net returns from farms in Canada which is comparable to that in the other provinces. The government has nothing more in mind to produce from the results of its policies than that result.
To come back to the position of the farmer, there is not a farmer from one end of Canada to the other but will say that his position is better under this government at the present time than it has ever been under any other government in the dominion. When I have said that I am not saying that the farmer has yet got all that is coming to him. That is the reason why we are saying tonight that we are not going to lower the return the farmer will receive as of the 1st of May or the first of any other month throughout the coming year. We have said to this house that we are going to establish prices for dairy products which will put the farmer in at least as good a position after the first of May as he had before the first of May.
This necessitates taking under consideration any increases that have been made in grain prices; it necessitates taking into consideration at the same time the fact that we have already increased the financial position of agriculture in all the provinces that produce live stock products as related to the provinces 83166-138
that produce grain. Not only have we done that as relating to the provinces that produce live stock to be fed grain, we have done that as relating to the provinces that produce grain in so far as they feed their grain to live stock.
Our province of Saskatchewan is not entirely a grain producing area. If one draws a line from the southeast corner of our province to Lloydminster he will find that the line runs about twenty miles north of Regina and twenty miles south of Saskatoon. It will be found that the area north of that line is a live stock producing area, just as important a live stock producing area as can be found anywhere in Canada. The hon. member for Melfort knows this. As was said earlier in this house during a debate, when he came back from the first war he made a trip across our country and searched for an area in which to establish farming operations. He chose the Melfort district in the northeastern part of Saskatchewan. If he has not very good judgment in his politics he certainly had good judgment in his choice of a farming area. He has a good farm in that area and he has done very well. He is in the centre of the live stock producing area of our province. I want to say again that that area is just as much a mixed farming area, a live stock producing area and a dairy producing area as any section of the Dominion of Canada. It can stand comparison with any other part of Canada both with regard to production and with regard to net returns.
The southwestern part of the province is a grain-growing area, and we can sit in this house and belittle the discussions that have taken place on wheat, as I have heard them belittled by the previous speaker; but, after we have belittled them as much as we can, we come back to the fact that there is no other product produced in Canada that is-shipped out in quantities to bring in as much outside money into Canada as wheat. Since that is the case, a considerable part of the business of this country is dependent upon the production of that area. It is not a wheat growing area by accident. It is the only product they can produce there to advantage and remain there and maintain their families on a reasonable standard of living. In other words, it is a natural grain growing area, not only for wheat but other grains. It is not an accident that they are producing grain there. They were able to go into that section of the country, stick a plough into the land and plough a whole quarter-section the first year and the second year have it under crop. Of course people who would go into an area of that kind would start growing grain.

Emergency Powers

The other sections went into mixed farming for the same reason that Ontario went into mixed farming. The northeastern part of the province was covered by trees, much of it not by trees big enough to call forests. We call them scrub, scrub poplar, scrub willow and trees of different kinds which had to be cleared. People who go into an area of that kind would naturally go in for mixed farming, because they are not able to make enough money in any other way on the small acreage they have to maintain them while clearing. They went into mixed farming and they remained in mixed farming. But neither the farmers in that section nor the farmers in the remainder of Canada could produce anything like the live stock they are producing today were it not for the fact that farmers did go into the grain growing area and did produce and ship large quantities of grain, the surpasses which made production possible. So I would say to any member of this house, farmer or no farmer, who lives in eastern Canada, that he is not doing credit to 'himself or to the farmers in his area when he decries the discussion of grain or wheat on the floor of this house; for it is a product which brings more wealth into this country than any other product, a product which makes it possible for live stock to be fed on farms right across Canada in the quantities in which is fed, a product which makes it possible for every province, except the three provinces that grow the grain, to have a higher gross income from farming last year that they ever had in any other year in their history.
Having said that, I come back to the chief criticism made by the 'hon. member who just took his seat. His chief criticism is that our production was down in 1946 as compared with 1944. I have given a partial explanation, 'namely that much that was sold in 1944 was not produced that year. But there is another thing I should like to say. My hon. friend speaks of what has been going on, the lack of planning, the lack of organization, the lack of leadership to the farmers of this country. I listened to that kind of speech during the first four years I was here prior to the war, and yet farm production went up and up year after year in spite of the fact that my hon. friend was making the same kind of speech that he did tonight. Then the war came. You can go back and check the record in the debates of this house, and you will find that every year he predicted that our production would go down and down. Yet from 1939 to 1944 it soared from one height to another, until it reached a record height in 1944 which probably no other farm group in Canada
(Mr. Gardiner.]
under any kind of organization or leadership will be able to match over a long period of
years.
There was a war.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not speaking now of the prices they obtained for their crop but of their production.
There was a demand for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend said there was a demand. All I will say is that we made a much better job in getting that demand when half the world was shut out from us than my hon. friend and his government did in the five years they were in power when the whole world was open to them to blast their way into. The situation from 1939 to 1944 was that we had only one market where we could market our products to advantage, and that market was the British isles. My hon. friend has been saying tonight: Yes, we are willing that the United Kingdom should be fed. But, Mr. Chairman, fortunately those who are administering affairs in the United Kingdom know a great deal more about agriculture in this country than the hon. member himself does, and because they do they are not misled by the kind of argument he was making a few moments ago, when he said that a few years ago we were selling 700,000,000 pounds of bacon to Britain.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The only reason you did not say it was because you could not remember the figures.

The minister may be the crown prince of Saskatchewan, but he is not going to bull-doze me in the House of Commons. He may do that in the little country schoolhouse, but I say that he has never heard me in twenty-five years state that we ever sold
700,000,000 pounds of bacon to Britain, and he knows that I know we never did. That was just a straight political statement of his, or it indicated senility or a misunderstanding of the facts. The minister cannot put that over. The minister knows better than anyone else; everyone in his department knows, and the leader of the C.C.F. party knows that I never at any time made the statement that we ever sold Britain 700,000,000 pounds of bacon, because I know we never had that much to sell. But in 1921 we sold 255,000,000 pounds. That is the statement I made.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not been listening very closely. I did not give

Emergency Powers
credit to the party of which he is a member for every having sold 700,000,000 pounds of bacon to anybody.
You said I said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I said we sold 700,000,000 pounds, and the actual figure here is 717,000,000 pounds.

In what year did1 you sell
717.000.	000 pounds?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will give you the whole record. In 1944-
What is the minister quoting from?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: From the official records of the statistics bureau of the dominion government.
How much are you selling them this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We shall get around to that in a minute. I am making this speech, and not you.
You are making your own, but do not make mine.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In 1944 we sold
717.000.	000 pounds of bacon to Britain. And after that experience we had sold or fed the enormous amounts of feed grain which were produced in 1942 and the amount we added to it in 1943 and also what we had grown in 1944. By the end of July, 1945, we had only one month's feed stored in the Dominion of Canada on our farms and elsewhere, with a new crop coming up. In these circumstances this government was wise enough to know that it was absolutely impossible for the farmers of this country to feed 717,000,000 pounds of bacon to go to Britain any time again until we had gone through the first three or four years of another war, or preparation for it, which would compel us to keep our grain stored in our bins year after year until we could open up a way for it into the natural markets of the world on the European continent. Therefore we began to plan for that. What did we do? We signed a contract with Britain not to deliver 600,000,000 pounds as we did the preceding year, when we actually delivered 717,000,000 pounds, but
450.000.	000 pounds a year. For the reason that we knew there were men in this country like the hon. member who has just spoken who would go out and say that was an indication that we wanted the farmers to decrease the production, we made a two-year contract for 900,000,000 pounds over the two years in
83166-138J
order that we might have two years in which to make the shift. True to form, my hon. friends in this house and all through this country went out and said that the government of this country is deliberately cutting down on supplies of bacon to Great Britain. My hon. friends said that we could never build it up. We did build it up from the unreasonably low levels at which it was in 1935 to the enormous quantity of 717,000,000 pounds sent in 1944. Then, when we reduce it to a figure that they never dreamed of being able to reach in their day, 450,000,000 pounds, they thought that was a ridiculous thing to do. Now, when they find that there is not enough feed in Canada with which to feed the live stock we now have they are still trying to maintain that somebody somehow could have been able to feed more hogs and more cattle in Canada. The only way in which we can feed hogs and cattle is to produce grain with which to feed them. Every bushel of feed grain that we have in this country is being fed in this year, which is an indication that we could not have produced more.
My hon. friend tries to lead us to believe that that reduction is due to some kind of policy which the present government has been following; but when anybody suggests that the reductions that came about from 1929 when they were going to blast their way into the markets of the world down to 1932 had anything to do with the Conservative policy in the country they say it is all bosh. I am prepared to accept his suggestion that the fact that we had a Conservative government here then was not the only reason for our bad times, provided that he will just say that the fact that our farmers have such good times now is partly because we have a Liberal government. I am quite sure that whether he will say that or not-
You hit a war, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, we had a war. We had a war before when my hon. friend's friends were in power. When that war ended what happened?
We had higher prices than we have today.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, you had higher prices for a few days. Wheat 'sold at S3.05 for one day, and during that time the government sold some millions of bushels of wheat and wheat went down like a rock and never came back.

Yes-
Emergency Powers

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I know, because I was selling wheat then off my own farm.
So was I.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: And it kept on going down, and we had a new government in power-
It went up, did it?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, wheat went up and kept on going up, until from 1926 to 1929 we had the best conditions in this country that agriculture had ever experienced prior to that time and the best conditions we have ever had since until the last four years. Both of these good financial conditions for the farmer were created, not under a Conservative government not under these ideas that we have listened to for the last two months, but under the policies that were put into effect by this government.
My hon. friend says that his hon. friends to the left of him are talking socialism. I quite agree that they believe in socialism, but more than half the time they are talking liberalism. The only way in which a government can really benefit the people of this country, no matter what they talk in order to get elected, is to put truly Liberal policies into effect while they are in office. When they do that the position of agriculture improves. Unfortunately for other parties in this country the only party that has ever done that is the Liberal party. Our position has always been improved under Liberalism.
I do not know whether this is going to develop into an old-time political campaign. It has been going on now for some months. I have sat here for two months, and during the greater part of that time I have been reprimanded both in the house and outside of it when I rose on a point of order in order to try to keep things in order. I have now come to the conclusion that the best thing I could do is to make a few political speeches myself, and that probably in making them we shall finally convince hon. members opposite of what I think is the truth. They are standing here day after day making speeches for no other purpose than to get free propaganda before the people of this country. I would suggest to my hon. friends that if they really do want an election, if they really do want to get political propaganda out to the country, just get together against the policies that this government is putting into effect, make a clear statement of their position in relation to them, say why they are opposing it and vote that way; if as they think they can find some support from this side of the house they may

get an election, and they will probably find out what the people really think about these matters. But may I say this to them-
Call one in Halifax now.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We who sit on this side know hon. members on this side well enough to know that they believe in Liberal policies. They believe in liberalism. They know that there is no other party in this country which would ever give them Liberalism in this country except the Liberal party. They are going to keep this party in power for some considerable time in spite of the talk of my hon. friends. I would suggest to them that, instead of putting on full-dress debates on the matter of paying subsidies for two or three weeks on a small quantity of butter and cheese that is put on boats when they come into port, we get down to discussing what is before us and continue to do that for a while.
One of your own members started it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, but I tried to stop him, and I am trying to stop everybody now. Let us get down to discussing what is before the committee and put these items through. Someone has been saying that they want to know what we are going to do about old age pensions. They want to know what we are going to do about other important matters. We have been trying to tell the house for two months that, just as soon as this bill is put through, it will know all about what we are going to do about these matters. The bills will be brought down and placed before the house and we shall have an opportunity of discussing them. If everybody is interested in these matters, then let us get on with this bill; pass it, get it through the house, get it out of the way, go on with the administration of it. Then we shall bring down the legislation which everybody seems to be worrying about and have it discussed, and let us get home some time this summer.

I am sure that the Minister of Agriculture does not need any assistance in meeting the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. In view of the fact that hon. members on this side of the house directed a good deal of heat in this direction, to keep the record straight a word should be said about the so-called wonderful days which existed when these hon. members sat over on the other side of the house. I was living in a part of Canada that took seriously the propaganda of a well-known Canadian who promised that he would blast his way into the markets of the world; that he would cure unemployment or perish in the attempt. That constituency

Emergency Powers
elected a supporter of that well-known Canadian and he became a member of the cabinet, but the blasting did not seem to click and the unemployment situation grew worse. Our young men left home to go east to look for work, and everywhere the situation was the same-no men wanted. The farmers took their butter to town, and I remember farmers taking that product home again, unable to sell it at ten cents a pound. One farmer brought thirty dozen eggs to town one day and received ninety cents-three cents a dozen, in the good old days when the Tories were in office. I am sure the farmers in all parts of Canada have sufficiently vivid memories to recall those days and they certainly do not want a repetition of those incidents.
A Labour government was in office in Britain at the same time.

Not very long. They never had a majority. The Minister of Agriculture said, quite correctly, that the Canadian farmers during the war period were in a more favourable position than ever before; they were in that favourable position when all our markets were gone with the exception of the British market, and for a very large portion of the war we were supplying agriculutral products to Great Britain, as part of the mutual aid programme, which meant in reality that Canadian farmers were enjoying prosperity, while they were participating in giving agricultural products away. I want to make it clear that we were in complete agreement with the government policy that made agricultural products available in Great Britain. Indeed, I am not very proud of the fact that some Canadians have come through the war in such a favourable financial position. While we made substantial gifts in inan-power and materials, when we consider the position which other countries of the world are in, we cannot take a great deal of satisfaction in the financial position of Canadians in many walks of life at the present time.
The situation is still unsatisfactory. I have in my hand the Canadian agricultural programme for 1947, which is published under the authority of the Minister of Agriculture. It refers to the fourteen agricultural conferences which were convened here during the war. At the last meeting the deputy minister of agriculture gave a report of a conference lie had recently attended at Copenhagen and mentioned that the world grain deficit was given as 8,000,000 tons, while there was a potential shortage of rice of about 6,000,000 pounds. Fats and oils were fifteen per cent below the pre-war average, and meat production dropped
in the war to seventy per cent of pre-war levels in Europe and sixty per cent in the United Kingdom.
I find in this report that, while we reached enviable heights in the field of dairy production, hogs and cattle, during the war, our production is now falling off. On page 21, I find that the hog production in 1946 had dropped to 4,350,000 as compared with 5,861.000 for the previous year. It indicates that the government wants an increase of nineteen per cent in 1947 over the 1946 production, and the statistics for the past two years would indicate that we are not likely to reach this objective.
I mentioned before the dinner recess that I visited my constituency in the Easter recess. I was told at several points that hog production is decreasing rapidly and that the farmers in that part of the country are not likely to go into hog production again. They say they are not getting a satisfactory deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
May I be permitted an interruption? On that point I must admit that I was taken away by some of the interruptions we had from something I was going to say and should have said. What I started to say at one stage of my remarks was that the figures which appear in our contracts are fully understood by the British and have been all the way through ever since we made the reduction to 450,000,000 pounds. We have discussed the matter with them and have also discussed the question whether we should reduce the figure to what we expect to be able to supply, or hold it at what we are trying to get the farmer to produce, and we have written into the contract what we have been trying to get the farmers to produce. It is necessary for me to make that statement because, if the matter is looked at from any other point of view, one gets a mistaken idea.
The British knew, for example, last year that, while we wrote 125.000.000 pounds of cheese into the contract they did not expect to get 100,000,000 pounds. They knew that beforehand.
The British house did not know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Their officials know it, and they can use their judgment whether they tell householders. But the objective put before them was that. If we had said to the farmers, "All that the British want is 100000,000 pounds," they might not have tried to produce 140,000,000 or 150,000,000 pounds. They might slip down, fearing that they would not have a market. So we put up the figure, and we said that in that way we would try to encourage the farmers to come up to the

Emergency Powers
standard the British desired. But the British always knew whether we were coming up to it or falling down, and they knew it weeks in advance.

During the war years, with over three-quarters of a million of the youngest and strongest men in the armed services and with a similar group producing armaments, Canadians did increase production of hogs, beef and milk. Now that the war is over, we are no longer engaged in the manufacture of munitions and our service personnel are back home. There must, therefore, be something radically wrong with the Canadian economy when the production of milk, butter and eggs declines. It is a reflection on our Canadian set-up that we cannot get our Canadian youth to take on the job of milking cows, feeding pigs and making butter. I think the only thing wrong is that the young people of Canada feel that those engaged in agriculture are not getting a fair share of the national income.
I agree with what the minister said earlier, that Canadian farmers are in a better position today than before. I think the debt position of the farmer in 1947 is better than it was at the end of the last war. But I was in British Columbia the other day at the C.C.F. convention, and when the agricultural policy was discussed I was amazed to hear delegate after delegate, as he rose, say, "I spent the first twenty, or thirty or forty years of my life on a farm and here I am now in Vancouver. I am not going to go back to the farm and I do not want my children to live on the farm". In Ontario the same situation prevails, certainly in that part of the province where I lived, in Bruce county. Very few-young people plan on taking over the family farm and continuing the production of agricultural commodities.
I submit that the minister has now sufficient evidence to know that the policy of getting rid of controls and subsidies will not enable Canada to meet her commitments to the hungry people of the world, with the very serious deficit of grain products, of meat products, of fats. I think we should be following the policy in agriculture which the minister of reconstruction followed during the war. He was not held up by lack of gold or lack of foreign markets. His programme was carried out on the theory that whatever is physically possible somehow or another must be made financially possible. I submit that the minister will not be able to supply adequate stocks of butter for Canada and abroad by leaving it to free enterprise or to supply and demand.

The farmers are the victims of huge monopolies which control the price of everything the farmer buys, and which in the past have controlled the price of things the farmers sold. Some of my hon. friends who sit to my right were here when the Stevens mass buying commission investigated price spreads, the operation of the tobacco industry, the canning industry and the packing industry. All down the line it was the same story. I remember that when you bought a can of peas or com you actually got about three-quarters of a cent's worth of vegetables, about three-quarters of a cent's worth of labour, and the rest went for the tin can which was thrown out, and profits that made huge fortunes for a very small group of people who operated on a monopolistic basis.
I submit that if Canada is to fulfil her commitments to feed the hungry people in the world the minister must use the weapons that he has to tax these corporations which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned the other day and see that subsidies, if necessary, are paid to producers so that we shall maintain our production and supply the home and foreign markets. I think the minister should make some statement before we take his advice and go on, as to his opinion regarding the possibilities of Canadian children being able to have enough milk to drink in the next few years if you leave it to the law of supply and demand, to see that they get enough wages in the pay cheques so that they can buy milk at the greatly increased price. If the minister has the statistics, I think he would be able to tell us that our local consumption of milk is going down markedly in the cities and towns across the country. Again there is something seriously wrong when our own children have to consume less milk in 1947 than they did in 1945 when the enemy threatened our commerce and our people were risking their lives all over the country. Before we leave this item, I should like the minister to give some indication that the consumer in Canada will be able to maintain his consumption of dairy products, meat and pork products on a level similar to that- which prevailed during the war.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to occupy but a very small portion of your time and to be as speedy as usual I do that in order to answer some of the things said by the Minister of Agriculture, and I take what he said in reverse order. The last thing that he said was that we on this side of the house were using this opportunity to put propaganda before the people of Canada. We may have some who are capable of doing

that, but since this is the first time that I have risen in this debate, either on the resolution, second reading or now in committee, I think I might be forgiven any such dastardly charge as trying to be political, particularly in view of the fact that the minister himself has made three political speeches on this very measure.

I give you my word that no one else can compare with the minister. He will keep on longer than anyone else; even though he does not say anything, he can still keep on going.
The next point he raised was this. He said my friends to my left, the state socialists, were talking liberalism.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

That about half the time the hon. gentlemen to my left were preaching liberalism. You know, Mr. Chairman, words change. There is a simple word called "planning", and I shall have something to say about that, too. speechtext: Order.

May I say that I shall answer both of you and all of you. One man mentioned "grafting", and if you mean what I think you did I will take you
on now or any other time. With respect to the word "progressive", I will take that on before I have finished. It does seem to me that the thing has become a bit threadbare and my hon. friends either need a new needle or a new record, because all they are doing is playing the old one again and again and it has become very scratchy.
So I come back to what I started to say, with the kindly interjections and help of my hon. friends over here, and that was that the minister said they were speaking liberalism- I am using his last explanation of what he said -about half the time. Let me accept that, if I know the meaning of the word liberalism. But I know another word a great deal better, and the minister and his government are not talking but are preaching socialism more than half the time, and they are acting it and practising it.
The next note I made with respect to what he said was on the position of the farmer today under this government, and he spoke of a levelling up of prices. I know about the farmer in the area in which I was born, where my grandparents farmed at a place called Foxley, twelve miles north of Regina where I spent all my boyhood holidays. I am certainly a blue-blooded fellow. My father was a tinsmith; he progressed and became a hardware merchant. My mother was a schoolteacher. I do know a little about the history of the country which these young fellows over here have now claimed to discover and all that sort of thing. It was there long before they knew about it. It was Assiniboia then. It is now the province of Saskatchewan. What I have in mind is this. All through the minister's speech he said "we" did this, "we" did that. I got lost in the millions. The most things I ever saw together-and I know nothing of dollars-was in a round-up where there were 30,000 head of cattle. To me that is a tremendous number of things. It is the most I ever saw in one place, but I have not been to a football match in England, for example, so that is the farthest I can go. But what struck me as amusing and with a little bit of resentment, was that the Minister of Agriculture through this war took full credit for what the farmers in this country did; and in my judgment the farmers did it in spite of the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Once he even told them to grow less wheat.

of doing at the moment is not to go into detail but to throw a blanket of obscurity over him because I think he would be much happier in that position.

speechtext: He really used to be a Tory, and you used to be a Liberal. You had better get together.

But if it were not for this man Bennett people opposite and people to my immediate left would be absolutely naked in their arguments in ninety-nine per cent of the subjects which come up in this House of Commons. Nothing.

Where did he stand in the world economy? I was in Ottawa in 1932, and I was very well paid for it. At that time I was acting in the Beauharnois inquiry before the senate committee.
