I am going to take care of this, in a much broader sense. There is no question that between 1929 and 1939 we had a depression. The expression "the terrible thirties" is one which, in my judgment, was wisely used, and I admit that frankly.
But what was the situation at that time in this House of Commons among right honourable and honourable members opposite-and I use those words in the same collation? We have been speaking of a man named Bennett, who is now a viscount. Someone asked a minute ago: Why did he leave this country? I think that came from over here to my left. Let us be fair about it. Let me say to hon. members on my immediate left, who believe in 'socialism, that I think they have an arguable position. I have never denied that. They have an economic theory under which they believe we can economically and socially better the position of our people. I accept that from them. I am sure the suggestion is made in all honesty; I have no doubt about that at all. So surely we can have our bits of difference with respect to economic and social theories without going back and saying that so-and-so did this in eighteen slixty-slix, or eighteen seventj'-six or eighteen eighty-six.
Eighteen slixty-slix?

The Minister of Agriculture does not know that I do that deliberately. That used to make a hit in the schoolhouse.
Is there anyone here who will deny that that was the first world-wide depression this world ever knew?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, I deny it. We went through one in the early nineties which was just as bad.
World-wide?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, world-wide.
I am sorry, but you must have read about that a lot later. You were not born at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I went through it, like a lot of other people.

I repeat what I said, and I have support to my left, 83166-139
although the Minister of Agriculture has a different view and a different memory.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You are more socialist than I am; that is all.
I think I am. And may I put it to you this way, that I am more honestly socialistic in my thought and in my heart than you will ever be. But you are a politician first and a socialist after.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I did not say "socialistic"; I said "socialist"; there is quite a difference.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He complimented you on your intelligence.

Well, I suppose there is a great difference between a noun and an adjective; but I always thought that socialist and socialistic persons were rather the same thing. However I appreciate the distinction the minister makes. What he means is this, by using the word "socialistic", that he loves all human kind, particularly if the3r are Grits. That is about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They are really better then.

That is about his socialistic position.
So I return again, Mr. Chairman, with respect to you and with your kindly permission, to this so-called depression. The depression then was a political one. It arose because every country in the world went completely nationalistic. It arose because countries like Great Britain, France, Italy and all the rest, after the first war decided that never again would they, if they could avoid it, be placed in a position where they had to import the greater [DOT] proportion of their food. That is what happened at that time. And so we had bad prices for farm products and so on.
I am not an economist and, in fact, I do not recognize anybody any more under that name except the Minister of Labour. I do not think those people really exist or are entitled to that appellation. What happened was that we all put up tariff barriers and walls and endeavoured to live within ourselves. The result was that world trade languished and almost died. Then we came to 1932, I think it was. I remember that expression which everybody now thinks was so funny, about blasting our way into the markets of the world. But I think hon. members will remember one thing about it; it won an election in any event and it is entitled to that much credit. The Ottawa

Emergency Powers

agreements were formed at that time and those are the Ottawa agreements having regard to this commonwealth.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, they were coming in here and taking out our gold, and this man Bennett had the courage to stop it on his own order and do more to save the economy of this country than any man sitting over there at the present time.
Pretty wide powers.

He took
the power and it was confirmed later. Let us be frank. I do not think I can be accused of going very far from the truth even though perhaps it may hurt me, or perhaps "hurt" is the wrong word to use. These things flow like water from a duck's back, although there ire no duck shooters here.
I close by saying I appreciate very much the fact that the Minister of Agriculture had a terrible loss during the war; I am not overlooking that in what I am going to say. I close with this: In the figures which he gave tonight covering from 1939 until the present day he did not give credit to the fact that we were at war, with respect to either production or prices. It is easy to say that we produced more then. We did. He asked the farmers to do it and they did it. Production of similar products was stopped in half the countries of the world.
I do not think we in this House of Commons can get any straight line. There is bound to be a complexity on one side and a complexity on the other side. As I said when I spoke first in this house, times have changed so much. I like the expression used the other day by the hon. member for New Westminster. He said that there were many who did not recognize that we had had a war which blew our country to pieces, that the lid had been blown off our economic life. I go with him in that. This is a time of changing economies. I have not any doubt of that whatever. I close by just saying: It seems to me to be bad business and bad faith to break with all the good that is in our past and try to have a new broom which will sweep clean, as the expression is. When you have done that there is nothing more to sweep. You will not have a broom left to sweep with.

May I again remind

(b) "subsidized goods" means creamery butter, eheddar cheese, concentrated whole milk products, white beans or yellow eye beans, or
fMr. A. L. Smith.]
such other goods as may be designated by order of the deputy minister of agriculture by notice in Canadian War Orders and Regulations.
We have discussed a great many things tonight, such as eggs, lumber and pulpwood. I cannot see where lumber and pulpwood would come within the definition of dairy products. Possibly eggs might, because I have often read that hens are milk fed, but I do not see how lumber could come within that category. It occurred to me that it is time now, after this wide discussion, to consider this order in council. I do not want to curtail the debate because I think it was with unanimous consent that the general discussion has taken place, but I submit that it is now time that we should deal with the order in council.
Mr. Chairman, you have suggested that we have been going around a large circle, but the circle has not been completed. I hope you will let me complete it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. mem-is correct. No member of the Social Credit group has taken part in the debate tonight. Would it meet with the wishes of all members of the committee that, after he completes his speech, we shall then deal with the order in council?

I am not going to speak at any length, but there are one or two things that have been said to which I should like to refer. The Minister of Agriculture has emphasized the fact that agriculture is better off today than it was before the war, and I agree with him. On the other hand, that it not saying very much, because agriculture was in a state of bankruptcy when the war came. As the minister said; the condition of agriculture could still be very much better than it is now. You have only to refer to the fact that agriculturists make up thirty per cent of the population, but today they receive only nineteen per cent of the national income. We still have a long way to go.
At the start of the war, farmers as a whole were heavily in debt; their buildings were depreciated and their machinery was mostly worn out. During the war, it was practically impossible to replace their machinery and now that they are trying to buy machinery they find- that prices have gone up considerably. We all know that the cost of building materials is very high at the present time.
During the 1930's we were constantly being told that we would have to be willing to produce at world prices, that we could not expect to get special prices in Canada. Shortly after the war started, when prices began to rise ceilings were placed upon the prices of agri-

Emergency Powers
cultural products. We were forced to receive world market prices before the war when world prices were low, but during the war when world prices went up we had to take lower prices. After a while the ceilings were raised slightly, but just at that time the income tax was increased greatly and the farmers were compelled to pay heavy taxes upon the repayment of their debts which had been incurred prior to the war. The result was that their debt charges were increased anywhere from thirty to forty per cent, and that places agriculture under a serious disability today.
I would say that what agriculture needs today from the government more than anything else is a declaration of policy to the effect that in the future the government will do all in their power to see that agriculture receives parity prices. When I refer to parity prices I am not talking about the wrishy-washy prices to which some hon. members refer; I am referring to prices that will return to the farmer his fair share of the national income, so that the income of the farmer will bear the same relationship to the national income as farm population bears to the national population.
The situation referred to this evening by the hon. member for Fraser Valley can be dealt with in only one way, by subsidy. I think that is the greatest mistake the government have made in their decontrol policy. They started off by taking off the subsidies, and then they took off the price controls. They should have left on the price controls and subsidies and then, taken off the price controls before the subsidies were taken away, instead of reversing the procedure as they have done. As a result, the cost of living for the people has gone up. I suggest to the minister that it is still not too late to reverse the policy and reimpose subsidies where they are found to be necessary, in order to maintain the purchasing power of the people.
I have been very much puzzled by the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party which emphasizes the need for the removal of all controls. If the party are sincere in that stand, when they suggest that all controls should be lifted they should also advocate that all tariffs be taken off because tariffs are controls. We all know, for example, that the seasonal tariff on fruits is a direct control. 1 quite agree that there are certain industries in this country which could not carry on without some form of protection. If any industry can show the government that it cannot continue without a tariff, let that industry apply for a subsidy and, if it is shown that the industry cannot produce in competition with imported goods, a subsidy could be paid. If that were 83166-139,}
done we would find that our eastern manufacturers would in future be a little more sympathetic toward subsidizing agriculture in western Canada. The eastern manufacturers have always been subsidized in the past by the tariff. We have heard a lot about the spoonfeeding of western Canada, 'but the manufacturers in the east have been spoon-fed right along.
By the shovelful.

Yes, by the shovelful. I know it will be said that a policy of that kind would cost a lot of money. I remember that this question of money was quite a serious one in this house before the war, but never once during the whole war were we told that we could not do this or could not do that because we had not the money. We produced the money, and by the shovelful, as someone remarked just now. But now wp are hearing the same old cry: it will cost too much to do this or to do that.
The hon. member for Stanstead the other day seemed to deplore the fact that our money had been diluted in relation to certain securities. I do not know just what he meant, but apparently he thought we were still on a gold basis. We are not on a gold basis, and have not been since the start of the war. After all, what is the value of money? It depends upon one thing alone, and that is its purchasing power. Personally I am far more interested in maintaining the purchasing power of the people than I am in maintaining the purchasing power of the dollar. The hon. member for Stanstead thought the value of the dollar had gone down too low. Would he suggest that we should reduce prices of agricultural products to increase the value of money? On what commodities does he think prices should be reduced in order to increase the value of money, because the only way we can increase the value of money is to bring prices down? When the Conservative party was in power in 1930 the dollar had a far greater value than it has today. Then it would buy four bushels of wheat or twelve dozen eggs. Surely the hon. member is not suggesting that we should increase the value of money today to what it was when the Conservatives were in power in the 1930's. I think it is far better to have the purchasing power of the dollar reduced and the purchasing power of the people increased to the point where they can buy what they want. So I would say that the only way in which we can decontrol in an orderly manner is to introduce subsidies in this country in order to maintain the purchasing power of the people at the point where they are able to buy the total production of the country.

This takes us back to the year 1927. I can see no reason in the world why the veterans preference could not be dealt with now. The Secretary of State told us some little time ago that he was going to bring down a separate bill with respect to the veterans preference. After all, it seems to me that one of the most important things in this country, now that the war is over, is that we should decide definitely and as soon as possible what these preferences amount to, without having to look through eight or ten orders in council and amendments. This particular order in council takes us back to the statutes of 1927, chapter 22, section 29, which deals with the preferences which are to be given in the civil service to the soldiers who served in the first great war. If hon. members will look through the order in council which we are now dealing with and those that follow they will find, as I found this afternoon in checking through them that they simply amount to adding some definitions and making some exceptions. I would ask the minister, is there any reason why this particular matter should not be dealt with now by a bill? Should not a 'bill be brought down now instead of later?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: A bill is to be brought down dealing with the veterans preference in the civil service and with other matters connected with the civil service which is not emergency legislation. speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is no present intention to set up a special committee to deal with civil service preference. Which we are now studying, by the way.
-will be the subject of additional specific bills later in the session. This would apply, for example, in the case of labour relations, which will be covered in a bill to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, orders regarding old age pensions which will be covered in a later bill to amend the Old Age Pensions Act and orders regarding veterans' preference in the civil service which will remain in the schedule pending examination of this subject by a parliamentary committee with a view to later introduction of legislation.
That is the language of the Prime Minister on February 4. It seems to me that that was a definite statement which was followed on the following day by another reply in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Royal as follows, as reported at page 130 of Hansard:
Mr. Mackenzie King:	On the matter of the
preference only.
Has the government now decided not to set up this committee?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Since I was the chairman of the committee in question, I might be permitted to say a word about this. This matter came up from time to time before the committee. So far as I remember, there was
pretty unanimous feeling that the preference as it then existed should be continued, and we so reported, as has been read by the minister. That was brought to the attention of the minister, and in view of the fact that there were a large number of committees and that hon. members were going to be very busy with other matters which had not been as carefully considered as this had been, the suggestion was made by several members of the house who were veteran members of that committee that a further study of the matter would not and could not carry us any farther than we had gone when we made our recommendation last year. I must say I was under the impression that all the members of the committee felt that they had gone as far as they could go in making that recommendation, and that no good purpose would be served by setting up a further committee on the matter. That is the state of affairs. I doubt very much whether any returned soldier members of the house really feel that a further committee could usefully be set up on this matter.

What did the Prime Minister refer to in the two quotations which I have read to the committee? I feel that there may be representations to enlarge the scope of preference perhaps to cover merchant seamen. I know I have had requests with respect to certain personnel in the women's service who are not covered by veterans' preference at the present time. I think that at least that should be studied by some committee. I am not prepared to say what stand they should take, but I believe that a committee might have served a useful purpose. How would the parliamentary assistant explain the statements made by the Prime Minister? I believe it was the Prime Minister's intention to proceed.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Before the opening of the session, it was the intention of the government to ask for the setting up of a special committee to study this matter. After the house met, it was found that many committees were to be set up, and it was also found that this would be a very controversial subject. It was thought that it would be in the best interests of the veterans to extend the preference as it existed rather than to reopen the whole matter. There were representations made to the government that the extent of this preference to a certain extent affected its value for individual veterans. There were also representations made that there were many who had wished to go overseas and who had been prevented by those in command of the forces here from getting overseas, and that, if the whole matter were reopened, it would be a very controversial subject because there
Emergency Powers

were many cases where strong representations were made to the government that the exclusion of the preference of such and such individuals whose cases were brought to our attention was working an unfair hardship upon them. It was felt that there would not be advantage to the veterans generally to reopen the question and that this extent to which the preference had been granted after the last war had brought about some difficulties, but that on the whole it worked reasonably well and that it was perhaps well at this time to attempt to continue it in that form rather than to break new ground.

Is it the intention to bring down legislation to put this into effect?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Just as soon as the time of parliament can be found to do it. As matters now stand, this emergency legislation requires to be dealt with before May 15. The public is anxious to have the budget announced. The budget is ready to be announced. After the Minister of Finance presents his budget, it is usual to take a certain short adjournment for the debate on the budget. All that time will be utilized. The legislation is ready to be put before the house just as soon as the house can find the proper time for considering it.

It will be brought down this session?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. The legislation dealing with this preference, the legislation dealing with old age pensions and the legislation dealing with labour relations will be brought down this session just as soon as parliament has disposed of these more urgent matters.
Let us get at it.

I do not wish to labour this point. I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the matter would have been controversial, and possibly that is the reason the government changed its mind. However, when the matter was discussed by the veterans committee last year, I do not think we came to any definite decision on it. There was an understanding that a committee would be appointed and that the matter of the civil service would be discussed later on, and for that reason the veterans committee did not deal with it conclusively. I would ask the minister this question. If a bill is brought down extending the civil service, will it include men like those of merchant marine and some others. I do not think it is necessary perhaps to have a committee to discuss this matter, but I would ask the minister if there is any 
intention of extending or enlarging the preference, or whether it will be left absolutely as it is at the present time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is intended to bring down a bill granting the same preference to veterans as included in the orders in council which extend the preference to veterans of this war. It is not intended to go farther than the order in council.

I support the remarks made by the hon. member for Royal, as a member of the veterans affairs committee of last year. The committee was very busy and rushed. When this question was discussed I am quite sure I am safe in saying that the members of that committee were under the impression that a special committee would be set up this year to deal with veterans affairs, and on that basis the recommendations were passed that were quoted by the hon. member for Rosthern. It is a question that should be referred to a committee. Representations have no doubt been made to the government. It is a question of making a second group for veterans who could not leave Canada, through no fault of their own, and there is the question of merchant seamen. I believe that women who joined the armed forces should receive preference in the government service, and I should like to see the government appoint a committee to study the matter.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We are discussing the procedure to be adopted when the bill is introduced later on in the session. That is a matter that can be discussed when the bill is introduced, but it need not be discussed now.

We are trying to indicate to the minister, that whether or not a committee is set up, we should like him to consider, when he brings down the bill to replace the order in council, the extension of the preference in certain quarters as suggested by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I had occasion recently, when in Vancouver, to speak to a spokesman for the merchant seamen, a student of the university of British Columbia. Although I know the department concerned has already ruled against their being put on all fours with veterans who served in the forces. I was quite unable, after talking to that man, to satisfy myself that the department was right in that decision. I could not find a proper distinction between a man who had served in a convoy, in the Atlantic, or going to Russia, and one who had served in the forces, and I believe there are many members who feel the same way on the subject.

Emergency Powers
I would urge the minister to consider a more extended bill than the one here. I am not talking about classifications but about those who would qualify as veterans under the new bill, and merchant seamen and the women's services, and one other class that has been mentioned. They are all classes that will get the support of many members.

I might mention the firefighters. I know of several instances where these men served overseas with the overseas fire-fighters and applied for positions with the federal fire-fighting services, and they were denied any right to the position because they had not had service in the armed forces overseas, although they had served with the overseas fire-fighting forces. That is one case where some consideration should be given.

The members in this group are prepared to let these orders in council get through as they now stand, but we still have not had an explanation which appeals to me as adequate, and it looks as if this discussion might be enlarged considerably because there are groups who have made representations for inclusion in the veterans preference. We have not been satisfied by the government as to why the selection of a parliamentary committee has been decided against. I have another quotation from the Minister of Justice. It seems to me that it was a definite undertaking on the part of the government as late as February 10. The Minister of Justice said that veterans preference legislation would be introduced this session, but only after the matter had been fully discussed by a committee of this house. We are prepared to let this go through tonight as it stands, but we have not had an explanation as to why we shall not be able to discuss the matter in committee.

May I ask the minister whether the legion or other veterans organizations have made representations to the government to have the matter discussed? There must be other organizations who have made representations asking to be included in the veterans preference, and I should like the minister to give a statement as to what organizations have asked.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I read a resolution that came in a few days ago dated March 27, 1947, from the army, navy and air force veterans in Canada. Among other resolutions there appears this one:
Whereas the commission on civil service salaries has recommended that veterans' appointment be modified,
Therefore be it resolved that the dominion government be requested to maintain this preference as it now stands in the statutes of this dominion.
That is the latest recommendation we have had.
Is that the only resolution with regard to veterans preference? Have any other organizations made representations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I would not say whether there have been any recommendations in previous years, but I have not had any within the last six months.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The Canadian Legion
suggested that there be a third preference for those who saw service only in Canada, and, as the hon. member will recall, our committee considered these other suggestions and decided that further extension of the preference would whittle down the value of it for those who already had it. After careful consideration, therefore, we made our report and when we considered the final report, as the hon. member will recall, we again considered this matter and decided that we would recommend that the preference as it exists at present be continued. Immediately I heard there was a suggestion that a committee be set up again this session, I pointed out to the government that our committee had considered this matter and made a definite recommendation. I presume it was in the light of that it was thought, since there were so many committees, and since our committee had considered it and recommended the continuation of the existing preference, that perhaps it was not the desire of the members to have a further committee on the subject. I spoke to several members of the veterans committee and they suggested that a further committee would not get us any farther than we got last year. That, I think, may have had some effect on the decision of the government to continue the existing preference, because our committee did consider the matter. I remember very well saying that, unless we had some desire to go farther than the existing preference, it would be taken that that was our final recommendation in the matter, and we so reported in the final report.

I merely want to ask one question with reference to these five orders in council, which I have not examined with the care that perhaps I should have given them. Do they apply only to the civil service, or do they apply to crown companies and other kindred organizations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Only to the civil service.
Emergency Powers
COMMO iS
Is there a veterans preference with respect to these other organizations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not under the Civil Service Act. I do not know whether there is under any other act, I do not think so though.
Do you not think it is worthy of consideration by the proper minister?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not when we are amending the Civil Service Act.

It seems to me that would be a very proper place to have it. Perhaps you might include in the Civil Service Act that these other persons are civil servants. In any event, may I make it merely as a suggestion to the proper minister of the government, that it might be worth while considering as to whether-it may be a fact; I am sure I do not know-the preference should not be given to other persons who are civil servants except in name only.

I want to admit that we were consulted at the start of the session as to whether or not we wanted a committee set up, but we felt at that time that nothing would be gained by it. As the hon. member for Rosthern has stated I think the reason is that we had representatives from the legion before us last year and they did make a recommendation regarding the second preference; but they were not at all sure whether or not they wanted that preference put into force, because they were afraid it might weaken the first preference. I felt that to have a committee at this time, without any certainty on the part of the legion whether they wanted the second preference put into force, would not get us anywhere. I think, before the government brings down new legislation, they should again consult the members of the former committee and see whether or not there has been any change in that opinion. I may say at this time that we are quite prepared to let these measures go through as they are.
Speaking on behalf of this group, may I say that I know of no one in it who was on the veterans affairs committee and who was consulted by the parliamentary assistant in this matter.
On the contrary, we were asked for names.

Yes, we were asked for names of members for the committee. I am
[Mr. C. W. G. Gibson.)
not saying, as far as we are concerned, whether we want the veterans' preference extended or not. But certainly we were given to understand that the committee was to be set up; we were asked for names of members for the committee and turned them in to the official government whip. Certainly there has been some change if the parliamentary assistant is to go around and consult those who he thinks will agree with him and not consult those who were on the committee who he thinks might disagree with him. I do not think that is a fair way of arriving at a conclusion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I really did not consult anybody. Several members of the committee came to me and said, "We discussed this last year at great length, and we came to a certain conclusion. What is this idea that we are going to thresh it all over again?" I said, "Well, I will bring it to the attention of the government that we did discuss it last year and that we did make a recommendation in the matter; then, of course, they will decide what they want to do." I was not under any commission to go around and consult people. Several members of the different parties came to me and made these representations to me; then I conveyed them to the government. If I had happened to run into my hon. friend at that time, I would certainly have asked him, because I got representations from practically every party, but perhaps I did not talk to him. They came to me rather than my going to them.

I am sorry to confess my ignorance, but may I ask the parliamentary assistant who has just spoken if there is any statute or order in council giving to veterans the preference in these various subsidiaries of the government, such as these crown companies, the C.B.C. and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
I know of none. Will you correct me if I am wrong?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I myself do not know of any, and that is one of the reasons why our committee made the recommendation which it did make, namely that the preference be applied to employment in the crown companies under the control of the dominion government and in regard to employment in this house as well as in the civil service; the recommendation was that the preference be applied throughout in regard to all people working for the government of Canada. We made that recommendation in our committee. So far as I know, up to this date I do not think there has been any change in the law in that regard.

Emergency Powers

That is all the more reason why this matter should be considered. If the crown companies being operated by this government are not giving any preference to the overseas men, then it is about time they did so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are. They always have done.
I know of several cases where they did not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I did not say that they were not giving the preference. I said that, as far as I know, by law they were not required to give it; but I am sure that they all do give the preference in that regard.
Mr. SMITH Calgary West): I am sure the hon. member will agree with me that it should be obligatory by law, should it not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is what we recommended.

I wish to correct an impression which I think the hon. member for Rosthern is trying to make in the house, namely, that the members of the veterans affairs committee are responsible for this civil service committee being dropped. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave the correct reason, namely, that it was a very controversial subject and that, as far as the members of the committee were concerned, they recognized that fact. It is not because we came to any agreement at all on the civil service. I am satisfied that most members of the veterans affairs committee expected that there would be some extension, though not the extension perhaps that a good many asked for; that is, that those in Canada receive the preference. I do not think there was any great demand in the committee for that. But they did feel that there were certain branches of the service, such as the ones I mentioned before, the merchant seamen and others, which should be included in the civil service. When we were told that there would be amendments to the Civil Service Act and that there a new act would come in, we fully expected that consideration would be given to these different branches of the service. I think the hon. member for Rosthern is trying to impress on the committee that we are responsible for the matter being dropped.

I do not think it necessary to come to the defence of the hon. member for Rosthern. I attended as many meetings of the veterans affairs committee last year as anyone else who was a member of it, but I cannot either argue with the remarks of the
last speaker or expand them, because that particular thorny question was considered in camera in that committee last >rear, and I shall not be the first to disclose those proceedings in it. But I am quite sure that I speak for a considerable number of the members of that committee when I differ in this respect only with the hon. member for Royal: I do not think the members of that committee expected that something would be done against their own recommendation. Probably the majority of the members of the committee were of the opinion that this particular problem, presenting the difficulties it did and having before them the diversity of opinion from the organized legion and other sources, were hopeful that the question would have a little time to resolve itself before they would be forced to come to a decision on it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall these items carry about the civil service?
Carried.
Call it eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Which ones are carried?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I should like to make this appeal to the members of the committee. Practically all the discussion that has been taking place on the item that we called has to do with a bill which is to be brought in and should be dealt with at that time. I would suggest that the members of the committee take this book; then, when we go into committee again they will have it before them and will see exactly what the item deals with. I believe we can save a good deal of time and conduct our business much more efficiently if each member knows exactly what we are dealing with and will try to stick to those items. I make that appeal because I believe that every hon. member wishes to make some progress in getting the business through the house.

Mr. Chairman, it was necessary that we know whether this committee is to be set up before we undertook to go into the details of five orders in council. It was for that reason I believe that most of us spoke as we did.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall I report progress?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; it is understood, is it, that the five orders in council headed "Civil Service Commission" are carried?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Yes.
